questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q16
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: Two reservoirs having different water levels are connected by two long parallel pipelines of same length and same material but having diameters of 600 mm and 400 mm. Using Darcy-Weisbach equation, the ratio of flowrate of water in the bigger diameter pipe to that in the smaller diameter pipe is
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Flow through Pipes (Parallel Pipes)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application (Bloom's Level 3)
  • Given Data:
    • Parallel pipes (same \(\Delta H\)); same length and friction factor (\(f_1 = f_2\), \(L_1 = L_2\)).
    • \(D_{\text{big}} = 600\) mm; \(D_{\text{small}} = 400\) mm
  • Aim: Find the ratio \(Q_{\text{big}} / Q_{\text{small}}\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Darcy-Weisbach Equation: \(h_f = \dfrac{f L Q^2}{12.1 D^5}\)
  • Parallel Pipe Condition: \(h_{f1} = h_{f2}\)

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Establish Proportionality:
    \[h_f \propto \dfrac{Q^2}{D^5} \implies \dfrac{Q_1^2}{D_1^5} = \dfrac{Q_2^2}{D_2^5}\]
  2. Rearrange for Ratio:
    \[\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} = \left(\dfrac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^{2.5}\]
  3. Substitute Values:
    \[\dfrac{Q_{\text{big}}}{Q_{\text{small}}} = \left(\dfrac{600}{400}\right)^{2.5} = (1.5)^{2.5}\]
  4. Calculate:
    \[(1.5)^{2.5} = 1.5^2 \times \sqrt{1.5} = 2.25 \times 1.2247 = 2.7556 \approx 2.76\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2.76  |  Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q17
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: An irrigation canal is to be designed to deliver 10 cumec to meet the peak demand of 7500 hectare of cropped area. The estimated canal losses are 50 % of the head discharge. The duty (in hectare/cumec) on capacity of this canal is
questions.explanation:
Irrigation Engineering | Water Requirements of Crops

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Peak demand discharge at outlet: \(Q_{out} = 10\) cumec (m³/s)
    • Area of crop: \(A = 7500\) hectare
    • Canal losses: 50% of the head discharge \(Q_{head}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the Duty (ha/cumec) on the capacity of the canal (based on head discharge).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Duty (\(D\)): Area of land irrigated by unit discharge flowing continuously throughout the base period: \(D = \dfrac{\text{Area}}{\text{Discharge}}\).
  • Head Discharge (\(Q_H\)): Discharge required at the canal entry, accounting for transmission losses.
  • Loss Relationship: \(Q_{out} = Q_{head} - \text{Losses}\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine Head Discharge:
    \[Q_{out} = Q_{head} - 0.50 \times Q_{head} = 0.50 \times Q_{head}\]
    \[Q_{head} = \dfrac{10}{0.50} = 20 \text{ cumec}\]
  2. Calculate Duty at Head:
    \[D_{head} = \dfrac{7500 \text{ ha}}{20 \text{ cumec}} = 375 \text{ ha/cumec}\]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 375 ha/cumec  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q40
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: For a hydraulic jump formed in a rectangular horizontal channel, the sequent depth ratio is 2. The Froude number of supercritical stream is
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Channel type: Rectangular and horizontal.
    • Phenomenon: Hydraulic jump.
    • Sequent depth ratio: \(y_2 / y_1 = 2\).
  • Aim: Calculate the Froude number of the supercritical stream (\(F_1\)).

3. Core Concepts:

Belanger's Momentum Equation: Relates depths before and after a hydraulic jump in a rectangular horizontal channel to the initial Froude number:

\[\dfrac{y_2}{y_1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8F_1^2} - 1\right)\]

where \(y_1\) = initial (supercritical) depth, \(y_2\) = sequent (subcritical) depth, \(F_1\) = initial Froude number.

4. Solution Method:

Substitute the given sequent depth ratio into Belanger's equation and isolate \(F_1\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Set up the equation:
    \[2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8F_1^2} - 1\right)\]
  2. Solve for the square root term:
    Multiply both sides by 2:
    \[4 = \sqrt{1 + 8F_1^2} - 1\]
    Add 1 to both sides:
    \[5 = \sqrt{1 + 8F_1^2}\]
  3. Square both sides and solve for \(F_1\):
    \[25 = 1 + 8F_1^2\]
    \[8F_1^2 = 24 \Rightarrow F_1^2 = 3 \Rightarrow F_1 = \sqrt{3}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(F_1 = \sqrt{3}\)  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: In a laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a circular pipe of radius 5 cm, the maximum velocity is found to be 2 m/s. The velocity (in m/s) at a radial distance of 2.50 cm from the axis of the pipe is
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Laminar Pipe Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Flow regime: Laminar; Fluid: Newtonian.
    • Circular pipe of radius \(R = 5\) cm.
    • Maximum velocity \(u_{\max} = 2\) m/s.
    • Radial distance of interest \(r = 2.50\) cm.
  • Aim: Find the local velocity (in m/s) at \(r = 2.50\) cm.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Hagen-Poiseuille Flow: For fully developed laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid in a circular pipe, the velocity distribution is parabolic.
  • Velocity Profile Equation:
    \[u(r) = u_{\max}\left[1 - \left(\dfrac{r}{R}\right)^2\right]\]
    where \(u_{\max}\) is the centerline velocity (at \(r = 0\)) and \(R\) is the pipe radius.

4. Solution Method:

Direct substitution of the given parameters (\(u_{\max}\), \(r\), and \(R\)) into the standard parabolic velocity profile formula.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify given values:
    \(u_{\max} = 2\) m/s, \(R = 5\) cm, \(r = 2.50\) cm.
    (Since \(r/R\) is dimensionless, cm/cm is valid — no unit conversion needed.)
  2. Compute the ratio \(r/R\):
    \[\dfrac{r}{R} = \dfrac{2.50}{5.00} = 0.5\]
  3. Apply the velocity profile equation:
    \[u(r) = 2\left[1 - (0.5)^2\right] = 2\left[1 - 0.25\right] = 2 \times 0.75 = 1.50 \text{ m/s}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.50 m/s  |  Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A fully-penetrating well of 20 cm diameter is provided in an unconfined aquifer. The height of the ground water table is 30 m from the bottom of the aquifer. After a long period of pumping at a rate of 63 m³/s, the drawdown in the observation wells at 10 m and 100 m from the pumped well is 12 m and 11 m, respectively. The transmissibility (in m²/s) of the aquifer is _______
(rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Groundwater Hydrology

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Well diameter = 20 cm; Aquifer type = Unconfined
    • Initial groundwater table from bottom: \(H = 30\) m
    • Pumping rate: \(Q = 63\) m³/s
    • Drawdown \(s_1 = 12\) m at \(r_1 = 10\) m
    • Drawdown \(s_2 = 11\) m at \(r_2 = 100\) m
  • Aim: Calculate the transmissibility (\(T\)) of the aquifer in m²/s.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Dupuit's Equation for Unconfined Aquifer:
    \[Q = \dfrac{\pi K (h_2^2 - h_1^2)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)}\]
    where \(h_1\) and \(h_2\) are heads from the bottom of the aquifer (\(h = H - s\)).
  • Transmissibility: \(T = K \times H\) (evaluated at initial saturated thickness).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Hydraulic Heads:
    \(h_1 = H - s_1 = 30 - 12 = 18\) m
    \(h_2 = H - s_2 = 30 - 11 = 19\) m
  2. Calculate Permeability \(K\):
    \[K = \dfrac{Q \ln(r_2/r_1)}{\pi(h_2^2 - h_1^2)} = \dfrac{63 \times \ln(10)}{\pi \times (361 - 324)}\]
    \[K = \dfrac{63 \times 2.302585}{\pi \times 37} = \dfrac{145.063}{116.239} = 1.248 \text{ m/s}\]
  3. Calculate Transmissibility:
    \[T = K \times H = 1.248 \times 30 = 37.4 \text{ m}^2/\text{s}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 37.4 m²/s  |  Accepted key range: 35.0 to 40.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A wide unlined channel carries sediment-free water. The depth of water is 1 m. The specific weight of water is 10 kN/m³. To prevent scouring, the maximum permissible tractive stress on bed is 10 N/m². The maximum slope of the channel bed to prevent scouring is 1 in n. The value of n is _______
(in integer).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics & Hydraulics | Open Channel Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension & Application
  • Given Data:
    • Channel type: Wide unlined channel
    • Depth of water: \(y = 1\) m
    • Specific weight of water: \(\gamma_w = 10{,}000\) N/m³
    • Maximum permissible tractive stress: \(\tau_c = 10\) N/m²
    • Slope: \(S = 1\) in \(n\)
  • Aim: Find the integer value of \(n\) to prevent scouring.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Average Boundary Shear Stress: \(\tau_0 = \gamma_w R S\)
  • Wide Channel Assumption: For \(B \gg y\), hydraulic radius \(R \approx y\).
  • Scour Prevention: \(\tau_0 \le \tau_c\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Applied Shear Stress:
    \(R \approx y = 1\) m
    \[\tau_0 = 10{,}000 \times 1 \times S = 10{,}000 S \text{ N/m}^2\]
  2. Equate to Permissible Stress:
    \[10{,}000 S = 10 \implies S = \dfrac{1}{1000}\]
  3. Solve for \(n\):
    \[S = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{1}{1000} \implies n = 1000\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1000  |  Accepted key range: 1000 to 1000

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A bridge with an expected life of 50 years is designed for a flood of 10000 m³/s corresponding to the return period of 100 years. The risk associated with this design is _______
(rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Flood Routing & Probability

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall & Application
  • Given Data:
    • Expected life of bridge: \(n = 50\) years
    • Design flood discharge = 10,000 m³/s
    • Return period: \(T = 100\) years
  • Aim: Calculate the risk associated with this design.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Annual Probability of Exceedance: \(p = 1/T\)
  • Probability of Non-Exceedance: \(q = 1 - p\)
  • Risk: Probability that design flood is exceeded at least once during life \(n\):
    \[R = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^n\]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate probabilities:
    \(p = 1/100 = 0.01\), \(\quad q = 0.99\)
  2. Calculate Risk:
    \[R = 1 - (0.99)^{50} = 1 - 0.60501 = 0.39499\]
  3. Round to two decimal places:
    \(R \approx 0.39\)

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.39  |  Accepted key range: 0.38 to 0.41

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q64
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The intensity-duration relationship for a rainfall on a rectangular plot ABCD of area 7 ha (1 ha = 10⁴ m²) can be modelled by the following equation:
\[I = \dfrac{25}{(t + 10)} \]
where \( I \) is rainfall intensity (in cm/h), and \( t \) is the duration (in minutes) of rainfall. The average runoff coefficient over the area is 0.60. The time of entry (in minutes) to the outfall from the corners A, B, C, and D is 10, 20, 15 and 25, respectively.

The design flowrate (in m³/h) of the storm-sewer at the outfall is _______
(in integer).
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Surface Water Runoff (Rational Method)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Area: \(A = 7\) ha \(= 7 \times 10^4\) m²
    • Runoff coefficient: \(C = 0.60\)
    • Rainfall intensity: \(I = \dfrac{25}{t+10}\) cm/h (\(t\) in min)
    • Time of entry from corners A, B, C, D: 10, 20, 15, 25 min
  • Aim: Calculate the design peak flowrate (\(Q\)) in m³/h.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Rational Formula: \(Q = C \cdot I \cdot A\)
  • Time of Concentration (\(t_c\)): Time for water to travel from the hydraulically most remote point to the outfall — ensures entire catchment contributes to peak:
    \[t_c = \max(t_{\text{entry}})\]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Time of Concentration:
    \[t_c = \max(10, 20, 15, 25) = 25 \text{ min}\]
  2. Critical Rainfall Intensity:
    \[I = \dfrac{25}{25 + 10} = \dfrac{25}{35} = \dfrac{5}{7} \text{ cm/h} = \dfrac{5}{7} \times 10^{-2} \text{ m/h}\]
  3. Design Flowrate:
    \[Q = 0.60 \times \dfrac{5}{7} \times 10^{-2} \times 7 \times 10^4\]
    \[Q = 0.60 \times \dfrac{5}{7} \times 700 = 0.60 \times 500 = 300 \text{ m}^3/\text{h}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 300 m³/h  |  Accepted key range: 300 to 300

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q19
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The Culturable Command Area (CCA) for a canal is 10000 hectares. The base period for a crop in the CCA is 140 days. Watering depth for the crop is 40 cm. The outlet discharge (in m³/s) lies between
questions.explanation:
Irrigation Engineering | Water Requirement of Crops

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Culturable Command Area (\(CCA\)) \(= 10{,}000\text{ hectares}\)
    • Base period (\(B\)) \(= 140\text{ days}\)
    • Watering depth / Delta (\(\Delta\)) \(= 40\text{ cm}\)
  • Aim: Determine the outlet discharge (\(Q\)) in \(\text{m}^3/\text{s}\) (cumecs).

3. Core Concepts:

Duty-Delta-Base Period Relationship:\[\Delta = \dfrac{8.64 \times B}{D} \]Where:

  • \(\Delta\) = Total depth of water required by the crop in meters (m).
  • \(B\) = Base period in days.
  • \(D\) = Duty of water in hectares/cumec.

Discharge Formula:\[Q = \dfrac{\text{Area}}{D} \]Where Area is in hectares, yielding discharge (\(Q\)) in cumecs (\(\text{m}^3/\text{s}\)).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert Delta (\(\Delta\)) from cm to m.
  2. Rearrange the Duty-Delta relation to solve for \(D\).
  3. Divide the given CCA by the calculated Duty to get \(Q\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Unit Conversion:
    \(\Delta = 40\text{ cm} = 0.4\text{ m}\)
  2. Calculate Duty (\(D\)):\[D = \dfrac{8.64 \times 140}{0.4} = \dfrac{1209.6}{0.4} = 3024\text{ hectares/cumec} \]
  3. Calculate Discharge (\(Q\)):\[Q = \dfrac{CCA}{D} = \dfrac{10000}{3024} \approx 3.307\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]The calculated discharge of \(3.307\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) lies between 3 and 4.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.307 m³/s | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q20
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Following statements are made with respect to the mass curve of rainfall:
(I) Slope at a point on the curve can be positive.
(II) Slope at a point on the curve can be zero.
Which one of the following options is CORRECT?
options: Statement (I) is TRUE and statement (II) is FALSE.
Statement (I) is FALSE and statement (II) is TRUE.

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: Statement (I) is TRUE and statement (II) is FALSE.
structuredOptions.html: Statement (I) is TRUE and statement (II) is FALSE.

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: Statement (I) is FALSE and statement (II) is TRUE.
structuredOptions.html: Statement (I) is FALSE and statement (II) is TRUE.

questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Precipitation & Rain Gauges

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Two statements regarding the slope of a mass curve of rainfall:
    • (I) Slope can be positive.
    • (II) Slope can be zero.
  • Aim: Identify the logical correctness of the given statements.

3. Core Concepts:

Mass Curve of Rainfall: A plot representing the cumulative precipitation (mm or cm) on the Y-axis against time on the X-axis.

Mathematical Properties: Because rainfall accumulates, cumulative rainfall is a monotonically non-decreasing function — it can never decrease.

Slope Meaning: The first derivative (slope) of the mass curve \(\left(\dfrac{dP}{dt}\right)\) represents the rainfall intensity (\(i\)) at any given time:

  • \(i > 0\): It is raining → Slope is positive.
  • \(i = 0\): It is not raining → Slope is zero.
  • \(i < 0\): Physically impossible → Slope cannot be negative.

4. Solution Method:

  • Statement (I): During a storm event, cumulative rainfall increases with time → slope is positive. (TRUE)
  • Statement (II): During dry periods (cessation of rain), cumulative rainfall remains constant → slope is zero. (TRUE)

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Statement I is physically valid, representing active precipitation.
Statement II is physically valid, representing periods of no precipitation.
Both statements are TRUE.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Both statements (I) and (II) are TRUE | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q32
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The probability (in %) that a storm having return period of 15 years may occur in the next 10 years is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Precipitation & Return Period

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Return period (\(T\)) \(= 15\) years
    • Design life (\(n\)) \(= 10\) years
  • Aim: Find the probability (in %) that the storm occurs at least once in the next 10 years (risk).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Probability of occurrence in any specific year: \(p = \dfrac{1}{T}\)
  • Probability of non-occurrence in a year: \(q = 1 - p\)
  • Probability of non-occurrence over \(n\) consecutive years: \(P_0 = q^n\)
  • Risk (at least 1 occurrence): \(P = 1 - q^n\)

4. Solution Method:

Substitute the values into the binomial probability framework.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate \(p\):\[p = \dfrac{1}{15} \approx 0.06667 \]
  2. Calculate \(q\):\[q = 1 - \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{14}{15} \]
  3. Probability of non-occurrence in 10 years:\[P_0 = \left(\dfrac{14}{15}\right)^{10} \approx 0.501625 \]
  4. Probability of occurring at least once:\[P = 1 - 0.501625 = 0.498375 \]
  5. Convert to percentage:\[P = 0.498375 \times 100\% \approx 49.84\% \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 49.84 % | Accepted key range: 45.00 to 55.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Types of flood routing and methods are given in the table below.

Column 1
Type of Flood Routing		Column 2
Method
(P) Hydrologic routing(i) Muskingum method
(Q) Hydraulic routing(ii) Modified Pul’s method
(R) Reservoir routing(iii) Method of Characteristics
(S) Channel routing

Option(s) giving the CORRECT match(es) between Column 1 and Column 2 is/are:
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Flood Routing

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: Two columns matching Flood Routing types to specific routing methods.
  • Aim: Identify ALL correct matching combinations (Multiple Select Question).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Hydrologic Routing: Uses the continuity equation only (\(\dfrac{dS}{dt} = I - Q\)). Methods: Muskingum Method (channels), Modified Pul's Method (reservoirs).
  • Hydraulic Routing: Uses both continuity and momentum equations (St. Venant equations). Methods: Method of Characteristics, Finite Difference Methods.
  • Reservoir Routing: Typically uses Modified Pul's method.
  • Channel Routing: Typically uses Muskingum method or Hydraulic methods (e.g., Method of Characteristics).

4. Solution Method:

Establish valid theoretical links, then evaluate each option:

  • (A) (P)–(i), (Q)–(iii), (R)–(ii): All pairs strictly valid. → Correct
  • (B) (Q)–(i): FALSE — Hydraulic routing does not use Muskingum. → Incorrect
  • (C) (P)–(i), (R)–(ii), (S)–(i): All pairs strictly valid. → Correct
  • (D) (P)–(ii), (Q)–(iii), (R)–(ii): All pairs strictly valid (Hydrologic routing includes Modified Pul's). → Correct

Note: In MSQ matching questions, any set containing individually true statements is a correct option. A 1-to-1 mapping is not required.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Evaluated Options A, C, and D — all contain only valid, individually correct mappings. Option B contains a false pairing (Hydraulic routing with Muskingum) and is rejected.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Options (A), (C), and (D) | Correct options: A; C; D

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Width (in m) of a rectangular channel required to carry a discharge of 96 m³/s at a critical depth of 9.8 m is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
Use acceleration due to gravity = 9.8 m/s²
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow (Critical Flow)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Channel shape: Rectangular
    • Total discharge (\(Q\)) \(= 96\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
    • Critical depth (\(y_c\)) \(= 9.8\text{ m}\)
    • Acceleration due to gravity (\(g\)) \(= 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\)
  • Aim: Find the required channel width (\(B\)) in meters (rounded to two decimal places).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Critical Flow in Rectangular Channels: At critical conditions (Froude number \(F_r = 1\)):\[y_c = \left(\dfrac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3} \]where \(q = Q/B\) is the discharge per unit width.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Rearrange the critical depth formula to solve for \(q\).
  2. Substitute known values to compute \(q\).
  3. Use \(q = Q/B\) to solve for \(B\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Solve for \(q\):\[y_c^3 = \dfrac{q^2}{g} \implies q^2 = y_c^3 \times g \]Substituting \(y_c = 9.8\text{ m}\) and \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\):\[q^2 = (9.8)^3 \times 9.8 = (9.8)^4 \]\[q = (9.8)^2 = 96.04\text{ m}^2/\text{s} \]
  2. Solve for Channel Width (\(B\)):\[B = \dfrac{Q}{q} = \dfrac{96}{96.04} = 0.9996\text{ m} \approx 1.00\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.00 m | Accepted key range: 0.90 to 1.10

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The cross section of a 0.5 m wide vertical gate holding water and oil is shown in the figure. The unit weights of water and oil are 10 kN/m³ and 7.5 kN/m³, respectively.


(Figure not to scale)
The horizontal hydrostatic force (in kN) acting on the vertical gate is _________ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Hydrostatic Forces

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Width of vertical gate, \(B = 0.5\text{ m}\)
    • Depth of oil layer, \(h_{\text{oil}} = 0.5\text{ m}\); Unit weight of oil, \(\gamma_{\text{oil}} = 7.5\text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • Depth of water layer, \(h_{\text{water}} = 1.0\text{ m}\); Unit weight of water, \(\gamma_{\text{water}} = 10\text{ kN/m}^3\)
  • Aim: Calculate the total horizontal hydrostatic force (kN) acting on the vertical gate.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Hydrostatic pressure variation: \(P = \int \gamma\,dz\)
  • For multi-layered fluids, pressure at an interface transfers down and adds to the underlying fluid's pressure.
  • Total hydrostatic force = Area of pressure diagram \(\times\) Width of gate.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Compute pressure intensities at the free surface, oil-water interface, and gate bottom.
  2. Calculate force on oil portion (triangular pressure diagram).
  3. Calculate force on water portion (trapezoidal pressure diagram).
  4. Sum individual forces.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Pressure Computations:
    • At free surface: \(P_0 = 0\text{ kN/m}^2\)
    • At oil-water interface: \(P_1 = 7.5 \times 0.5 = 3.75\text{ kN/m}^2\)
    • At gate bottom: \(P_2 = 3.75 + (10 \times 1.0) = 13.75\text{ kN/m}^2\)
  2. Force on oil portion (triangle):\[F_{\text{oil}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times P_1 \times h_{\text{oil}} \times B = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3.75 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.469\text{ kN} \]
  3. Force on water portion (trapezoid):\[F_{\text{water}} = \dfrac{P_1 + P_2}{2} \times h_{\text{water}} \times B = \dfrac{3.75 + 13.75}{2} \times 1.0 \times 0.5 = 8.75 \times 0.5 = 4.375\text{ kN} \]
  4. Total Force:\[F = F_{\text{oil}} + F_{\text{water}} = 0.469 + 4.375 = 4.844\text{ kN} \approx 4.84\text{ kN} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 4.84 kN | Accepted key range: 4.75 to 5.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A centrifugal pump is delivering water from an underground tank to an overhead reservoir against a static head of 35 m through a 2 km long, 250 mm diameter pipe. The head-discharge characteristic of the pump is given by
\[H = 140 - 9000Q^2 \]
where H is the head (in m) generated by the pump and Q is the discharge (in m³/s) of the pump.
Neglecting all minor losses, the head (in m) generated by the pump is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
Use: Darcy-Weisbach friction factor f = 0.04
Acceleration due to gravity = 9.81 m/s²
\( \pi = 3.14 \)
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pipe Flow & Pumps

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Static head: \(H_{\text{stat}} = 35\text{ m}\)
    • Pipe length: \(L = 2000\text{ m}\), Diameter: \(D = 0.25\text{ m}\)
    • Pump characteristic: \(H = 140 - 9000Q^2\)
    • Friction factor: \(f = 0.04\), \(g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2\), \(\pi = 3.14\)
    • Minor losses neglected.
  • Aim: Determine the head generated by the pump (\(H\) in m), rounded to nearest integer.

3. Core Concepts:

  • System Head: \(H_{\text{sys}} = H_{\text{stat}} + h_f\)
  • Darcy-Weisbach: \(h_f = \dfrac{8fLQ^2}{\pi^2 g D^5}\)
  • Operating Point: \(H_{\text{pump}} = H_{\text{sys}}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Express \(h_f\) as a function of \(Q^2\).
  2. Write the system head equation.
  3. Equate to pump characteristic and solve for \(Q^2\).
  4. Substitute \(Q^2\) back into pump equation to find \(H\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Friction Head Loss Coefficient:\[h_f = \dfrac{8 \times 0.04 \times 2000}{(3.14)^2 \times 9.81 \times (0.25)^5} \times Q^2 = \dfrac{640}{0.09446} Q^2 \approx 6775.66\,Q^2 \]
  2. System Head:\[H_{\text{sys}} = 35 + 6775.66\,Q^2 \]
  3. Operating Point:\[140 - 9000Q^2 = 35 + 6775.66Q^2 \]\[105 = 15775.66\,Q^2 \implies Q^2 = \dfrac{105}{15775.66} \approx 0.006656\text{ m}^6/\text{s}^2 \]
  4. Head Generated:\[H = 140 - 9000 \times 0.006656 = 140 - 59.90 = 80.10\text{ m} \approx 80\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 80 m | Accepted key range: 78 to 82

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The flow depth for a discharge of 10 m³/s in a wide rectangular channel is 2.0 m. Assume that the flow is uniform.
If the discharge is doubled, the flow depth (in m) in this channel is _________ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Open Channel Flow | Uniform Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Channel type: Wide rectangular
    • Initial: \(Q_1 = 10\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\), \(y_1 = 2.0\text{ m}\)
    • Final: \(Q_2 = 20\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) (doubled)
    • Flow is uniform; \(S\), \(B\), \(n\) are constant.
  • Aim: Calculate the new uniform flow depth \(y_2\) in meters.

3. Core Concepts:

  • For a wide rectangular channel: hydraulic radius \(R \approx y\).
  • Manning's Equation: \(Q = \dfrac{B}{n} y^{5/3} \sqrt{S}\)
  • Since \(B\), \(n\), and \(S\) are constant: \(Q \propto y^{5/3}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Set up ratio using Manning's proportionality.
  2. Substitute knowns and solve for \(y_2\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Ratio Setup:\[\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{y_1}\right)^{5/3} \implies \dfrac{20}{10} = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{2.0}\right)^{5/3} \]
  2. Solve for \(y_2\):\[2 = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{2.0}\right)^{5/3} \]Taking power \(3/5\) on both sides:\[\dfrac{y_2}{2.0} = 2^{3/5} = 2^{0.6} \approx 1.5157 \]\[y_2 = 2.0 \times 1.5157 = 3.031\text{ m} \approx 3.03\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.03 m | Accepted key range: 3.00 to 3.20

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q19
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: For a flowing fluid, a dimensionless combination of velocity (V), length scale (l), and acceleration due to gravity (g) would be
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Dimensional Analysis

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Velocity \(V\), length scale \(l\), and acceleration due to gravity \(g\).
  • Aim: Identify the correct dimensionless combination of these variables.

Core Concepts:

Dimensional Homogeneity: A true dimensionless number has no net fundamental dimensions (\(M^0L^0T^0\)).

Froude Number (\(Fr\)): A standard dimensionless parameter relating inertial forces to gravitational forces: \(Fr = \dfrac{V}{\sqrt{gl}}\). Squaring this yields another valid dimensionless combination.

Solution:

First, check the dimensions of each variable: \([V] = LT^{-1}\), \([l] = L\), \([g] = LT^{-2}\). Then evaluate each option:

  1. Option A \(\left(\dfrac{V^2}{gl}\right)\):
    \( \dfrac{(LT^{-1})^2}{L \cdot LT^{-2}} = \dfrac{L^2T^{-2}}{L^2T^{-2}} = L^0T^0 \)✓ This is dimensionless.
  2. Option B \(\left(\dfrac{Vg}{l}\right)\): \(\dfrac{LT^{-1} \cdot LT^{-2}}{L} = LT^{-3}\) — Not dimensionless.
  3. Option C \(\left(\dfrac{gl^2}{V}\right)\): \(\dfrac{LT^{-2} \cdot L^2}{LT^{-1}} = L^2T^{-1}\) — Not dimensionless.
  4. Option D \(\left(\dfrac{l}{V^2g}\right)\): \(\dfrac{L}{L^2T^{-2} \cdot LT^{-2}} = L^{-2}T^{4}\) — Not dimensionless.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\dfrac{V^2}{gl}\) | Option: A

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q20
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
To derive the total flood hydrograph at a catchment outlet from an isolated storm, the order in which the following methods are applied, from the first method to the last method, is

P. Obtaining the hyetograph
Q. Addition of baseflow
R. Estimation of initial and infiltration losses
S. Application of unit hydrograph
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Hydrograph Analysis

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Four steps in hydrograph analysis:
    P — Hyetograph
    Q — Baseflow addition
    R — Infiltration estimation
    S — Unit hydrograph application
  • Aim: Order the steps to derive a total flood hydrograph from an isolated storm.

Core Concepts:

Runoff Generation: Total rainfall minus losses (infiltration) equals effective rainfall.

Hydrograph Components: Direct Runoff Hydrograph (DRH) is obtained by applying the Unit Hydrograph (UH) to the effective rainfall. Total flood hydrograph = DRH + Baseflow.

Solution:

  1. Step 1 — P (Hyetograph): First, obtain the rainfall data over time (hyetograph).
  2. Step 2 — R (Infiltration estimation): Estimate initial and infiltration losses and subtract from the hyetograph to get the Effective Rainfall Hyetograph (ERH).
  3. Step 3 — S (Unit hydrograph application): Apply the unit hydrograph to the ERH to compute the Direct Runoff Hydrograph (DRH).
  4. Step 4 — Q (Baseflow addition): Add the baseflow to the DRH to obtain the total flood hydrograph.

The correct sequence is \(P \rightarrow R \rightarrow S \rightarrow Q\).

Final Answer:

Final Answer: PRSQ | Option: A

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q30
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: For the Bernoulli’s equation to be applicable in a fluid flow situation, which of the following conditions is/are to be satisfied:
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Applicability Conditions of Bernoulli’s Equation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    A set of proposed conditions for applying Bernoulli’s equation in a fluid-flow situation:
    (A) frictionless, (B) incompressible, (C) steady, (D) rotational.
  • Aim: Identify the condition(s) that must be satisfied for Bernoulli’s equation to be applicable.

Core Concepts

1) Origin of Bernoulli’s equation: It is obtained by integrating Euler’s equation along a streamline for an inviscid (frictionless) flow. For the commonly used engineering form between two points, it is written as\[\dfrac{p}{\gamma} + \dfrac{V^2}{2g} + z = \text{constant} \]

2) Required conditions (engineering form):

  • Frictionless (inviscid): Viscous dissipation must be negligible; otherwise head loss terms must be added.
  • Incompressible: Density \( ho\) is constant (valid for liquids and low-speed gas flows where density change is negligible).
  • Steady: Flow properties do not change with time at a fixed point, so the energy balance remains time-invariant.

3) Rotational vs irrotational:
For a rotational flow, Bernoulli’s constant can differ from one streamline to another; the equation is still valid along a given streamline (subject to inviscid, incompressible, steady conditions). For the strongest/general statement “applicable in a flow situation” (i.e., usable between arbitrary points without specifying same streamline), the flow should be irrotational, not rotational. Therefore, “flow should be rotational” is not a required condition and is generally the opposite of the added requirement for global applicability.

Standard assumptions: No shaft work addition/removal (no pumps/turbines between points) and no heat transfer effects in the mechanical energy form (typical GATE Bernoulli context).

Solution Method

  • Logic flow: (i) Recall derivation assumptions of Bernoulli from Euler equation, (ii) list mandatory assumptions, (iii) evaluate each option against these assumptions.
  • Alternative: Compare with extended energy equation: if friction exists, add head loss \(h_f\); if unsteady or compressible, additional terms/relations are needed.
  • Common pitfalls to avoid:
    (i) Thinking “rotational” is required; actually “irrotational” is the extra condition for same constant across streamlines.
    (ii) Forgetting that inviscid is essential for the simple Bernoulli form without head loss.

Step-by-Step Execution

  1. Check option (A): frictionless
    Bernoulli’s equation in its basic form assumes negligible viscosity (no frictional head loss). Hence (A) is required.
  2. Check option (B): incompressible
    The standard Bernoulli form \(p/\gamma + V^2/(2g) + z\) assumes constant density (incompressible). Hence (B) is required.
  3. Check option (C): steady
    Classical Bernoulli derivation assumes steady flow so that the energy per unit weight is time-invariant along the streamline. Hence (C) is required.
  4. Check option (D): rotational
    Rotational flow is not a requirement. In fact, to apply Bernoulli between any two points irrespective of streamline, the flow should be irrotational. Therefore “flow should be rotational” is not a condition to be satisfied. Hence (D) is not selected.

Validation & Error Handling:
Sanity check: The selected conditions match the standard GATE/undergraduate statement for Bernoulli applicability (inviscid, incompressible, steady). Excluding (D) is consistent because rotationality restricts Bernoulli to streamline-wise use rather than being a required prerequisite.

Final Answer

Final Answer: Conditions (A), (B), and (C) must be satisfied | Option(s): A, B, C

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A water resources project with an expected life of 25 years has to be designed for an acceptable risk of 5% against a design flood. The return period for the design flood (in years) is _______________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Flood Risk & Return Period

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Expected project life \(n\) = 25 years
    Acceptable risk \(R\) = 5% = 0.05
  • Aim: Return period (\(T\)) of the design flood (rounded off to nearest integer).

Core Concepts:

Risk \(R\) = probability that the design flood will be exceeded at least once in \(n\) years.

\[R = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^n \]

Standard in hydrological design of water resources projects (IS 6966 for dams, IRC guidelines for bridges).

Solution:

  1. Substitute known values:
    \[0.05 = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^{25} \]
    \[\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^{25} = 0.95 \]
  2. Take the 25th root of both sides:
    \[1 - \dfrac{1}{T} = 0.95^{1/25} \]
  3. Evaluate:
    \[0.95^{1/25} = 0.99795037 \]
  4. Solve for \(T\):
    \[\dfrac{1}{T} = 1 - 0.99795037 = 0.00204963 \]
    \[T = \dfrac{1}{0.00204963} \approx 487.89 \text{ years} \]
  5. Rounded to nearest integer = 488 years
    Note: Approximate formula for small R gives \(T \approx n/R = 500\) years; both lie in the official accepted range.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 488 | (Range 476 to 500)

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q39
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The mean rainfall over a catchment has to be estimated. The data for four rain gauges located in and around the catchment is listed in the table. Which one of the following statements is correct:

Rain gauge stationPQRS
Whether located inside the catchmentYesYesYesNo
Thiessen weightage factor0.250.500.100.15
Rainfall (mm)100110100125
options: The estimate obtained from the Thiessen-mean method is greater than that obtained using the arithmetic-mean method
The estimate obtained from the Thiessen-mean method is equal to that obtained using the arithmetic-mean method
The estimate obtained from the Thiessen-mean method is less than that obtained using the arithmetic-mean method
The Thiessen-mean method cannot be applied in this case

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: The estimate obtained from the Thiessen-mean method is greater than that obtained using the arithmetic-mean method
structuredOptions.html: The estimate obtained from the Thiessen-mean method is greater than that obtained using the arithmetic-mean method

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: The estimate obtained from the Thiessen-mean method is equal to that obtained using the arithmetic-mean method
structuredOptions.html: The estimate obtained from the Thiessen-mean method is equal to that obtained using the arithmetic-mean method

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: The estimate obtained from the Thiessen-mean method is less than that obtained using the arithmetic-mean method
structuredOptions.html: The estimate obtained from the Thiessen-mean method is less than that obtained using the arithmetic-mean method

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: The Thiessen-mean method cannot be applied in this case
structuredOptions.html: The Thiessen-mean method cannot be applied in this case

questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Precipitation & Rain Gauges

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    GaugeLocationWeightRainfall (mm)
    PInside catchment0.50110
    QInside catchment0.10100
    RInside catchment0.25100
    SOutside catchment0.15125
  • Aim: Compare mean rainfall estimated using the Thiessen-mean method versus the arithmetic-mean method.

Core Concepts:

Arithmetic Mean Method: Averages the rainfall depths of gauges located strictly inside the catchment only. Ignores spatial distribution.

Thiessen Polygon Method: Assigns area-based weights to each gauge (including nearby outside gauges influencing the catchment).

\[P_{avg} = \sum (P_i \times W_i) \]

Solution:

  1. Arithmetic Mean (gauges P, Q, R only — inside catchment):
    \[P_{arithmetic} = \dfrac{110 + 100 + 100}{3} = \dfrac{310}{3} = 103.33 \text{ mm} \]
  2. Thiessen Mean (all four gauges with given weights):
    \[P_{thiessen} = (110 \times 0.50) + (100 \times 0.10) + (100 \times 0.25) + (125 \times 0.15) \]
    \[P_{thiessen} = 55 + 10 + 25 + 18.75 = 108.75 \text{ mm} \]
  3. Comparison: Since 108.75 mm > 103.33 mm, the Thiessen-mean estimate is greater than the arithmetic-mean estimate. This is because gauge S (outside, highest rainfall of 125 mm) contributes a 15% weight in the Thiessen method but is excluded from the arithmetic mean.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: The Thiessen-mean estimate (108.75 mm) is greater than the arithmetic-mean estimate (103.33 mm) | Option: A

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Lacey’s regime equations, followed in India for making scour calculations while designing hydraulic structures across alluvial channels, are given below. Regarding these equations, which of the following statements is/are true:
\( D = 0.470 \times \left[\dfrac{Q}{f_s} \right]^{1/3} \)
\( P = 4.75 \times \sqrt{Q} \)
\( f_s = 1.76 \times \sqrt{d} \)
where, Q is discharge and \( f_s \) is silt factor.
options: D is the depth of scour below the existing riverbed
P is the Lacey’s waterway width
d is the average grain size diameter of the bed material in centimetres
D is the depth of scour below the design flood level

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: D is the depth of scour below the existing riverbed
structuredOptions.html: D is the depth of scour below the existing riverbed

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: P is the Lacey’s waterway width
structuredOptions.html: P is the Lacey’s waterway width

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: d is the average grain size diameter of the bed material in centimetres
structuredOptions.html: d is the average grain size diameter of the bed material in centimetres

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: D is the depth of scour below the design flood level
structuredOptions.html: D is the depth of scour below the design flood level

questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Lacey's Regime Theory

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Aim: Identify correct definitions of variables in Lacey's regime equations.
  • Given Equations:
    \[ D = 0.470 \times \left[\dfrac{Q}{f_s}\right]^{1/3} \]
    \[P = 4.75 \times \sqrt{Q} \]
    \[f_s = 1.76 \times \sqrt{d} \]

Core Concepts:

According to Lacey's regime theory (referenced in IS 6966 for scour depth calculations):

  • \(D\): Normal depth of scour measured below the design flood level (HFL), not from the existing riverbed.
  • \(P\): Wetted perimeter, closely approximating the clear waterway width required in regime condition.
  • \(d\): Average grain size diameter of bed material — must be input in millimeters (mm) for the silt factor formula.

Solution:

  1. Statement (A): Scour depth \(D\) is measured from the existing riverbed — False. It is measured from the design flood level (HFL).
  2. Statement (B): \(P\) defines Lacey's regime waterway width — True.
  3. Statement (C): \(d\) in \(f_s = 1.76\sqrt{d}\) is in centimetres — False. \(d\) must be in millimeters.
  4. Statement (D): \(D\) is the normal scour depth below HFL — True.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: Statements (B) and (D) are true | Option: B; D

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q60
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A hydraulic jump is formed in a 5 m wide rectangular channel, which has a horizontal bed and is carrying a discharge of 15 m³/s. The depth of water upstream of the jump is 0.5 m. The power dissipated by the jump (in kW) is _______________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
Note:
Acceleration due to gravity = 9.81 m/s²
Density of water = 1000 kg/m³
Kinetic energy correction factor = 1.0
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow / Hydraulic Jump

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Rectangular channel width \(B = 5\) m, Discharge \(Q = 15\) m³/s
    Upstream depth \(y_1 = 0.5\) m, \(g = 9.81\) m/s², \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m³
  • Aim: Calculate power dissipated by the hydraulic jump in kW (nearest integer).

Core Concepts:

  • Unit discharge: \(q = Q/B\)
  • Upstream Froude number: \(Fr_1^2 = \dfrac{q^2}{g y_1^3}\)
  • Conjugate depth (Belanger equation): \(\dfrac{y_2}{y_1} = \dfrac{1}{2}(\sqrt{1+8Fr_1^2}-1)\)
  • Head loss: \(h_L = \dfrac{(y_2-y_1)^3}{4y_1 y_2}\)
  • Power dissipated: \(P = \rho g Q h_L\)

Solution:

  1. Unit discharge and Froude number:
    \[q = \dfrac{15}{5} = 3 \text{ m}^2\text{/s} \]
    \[Fr_1^2 = \dfrac{3^2}{9.81 \times 0.5^3} = \dfrac{9}{1.22625} = 7.339 \]
  2. Post-jump depth \(y_2\):
    \[y_2 = \dfrac{0.5}{2}(\sqrt{1 + 8 \times 7.339} - 1) = 0.25(\sqrt{59.712} - 1) = 0.25(7.727 - 1) = 1.682 \text{ m} \]
  3. Head Loss:
    \[h_L = \dfrac{(1.682 - 0.5)^3}{4 \times 0.5 \times 1.682} = \dfrac{(1.182)^3}{3.364} = \dfrac{1.651}{3.364} = 0.4908 \text{ m} \]
  4. Power Dissipated:
    \[P = \dfrac{1000 \times 9.81 \times 15 \times 0.4908}{1000} = 72.22 \text{ kW} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 72 kW | Acceptable Range: 69 to 75

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q61
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A symmetrical trapezoidal canal is 100 km long. The bottom width is 10 m and the side slope is 1 Horizontal : 1 Vertical. The average flow depth in the canal is 2.5 m throughout the month of April. The measurement from a Class-A evaporimeter in the vicinity of the canal indicated an average evaporation rate of 0.5 cm/day in April.
The volume of water evaporated from the canal (in m³) in the month of April is close to _______________ ×10³ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Evaporation Losses / Canal Surface

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Trapezoidal canal: Length \(L = 100\) km, Bottom width \(B = 10\) m
    Side slope \(m = 1H:1V\), Flow depth \(y = 2.5\) m
    Month: April (30 days), Pan evaporation \(E_{pan} = 0.5\) cm/day
  • Aim: Volume of water evaporated in April in \(10^3\) m³, rounded to 1 decimal place.

Core Concepts:

Canal Top Width: \(T = B + 2my\) — evaporation occurs only from the free water surface.

Pan Coefficient (\(C_p\)): IS Code standardises \(C_p \approx 0.70\) for Class A pan to convert pan evaporation to actual lake/open water evaporation.

\[E_{lake} = C_p \times E_{pan} \]

Solution:

  1. Top width and surface area:
    \[T = 10 + 2 \times 1 \times 2.5 = 15 \text{ m} \]
    \[A_s = 15 \times 100{,}000 = 1{,}500{,}000 \text{ m}^2 \]
  2. Actual evaporation depth for April:
    \[E_{lake} = 0.70 \times 0.005 \text{ m/day} = 0.0035 \text{ m/day} \]
    Total depth \(= 0.0035 \times 30 = 0.105\) m
  3. Evaporated Volume:
    \[V = 1{,}500{,}000 \times 0.105 = 157{,}500 \text{ m}^3 = 157.5 \times 10^3 \text{ m}^3 \]

Note: The wide official range (120.0 to 180.0) accommodates slight variation in pan coefficients (0.7–0.8).

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 157.5 × 10³ m³ | Acceptable Range: 120.0 to 180.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q62
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A 5.0 m wide rectangular channel carries a discharge of 10 m³/s at a depth of 1.5 m under uniform flow. To produce critical flow conditions without affecting the upstream conditions, the channel bottom elevation should be raised (in m) by _______________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
Assume that there is no loss of head at the raise, kinetic energy correction factor is 1.0, and acceleration due to gravity is 9.81 m/s².
questions.explanation:
Open Channel Flow | Specific Energy & Channel Transitions / Hump Design

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Rectangular channel: \(B = 5.0\) m, \(Q = 10\) m³/s
    Upstream depth \(y_1 = 1.5\) m, Head loss = 0, \(g = 9.81\) m/s²
  • Aim: Find height of channel bottom raise \(\Delta Z\) to produce critical flow without altering upstream conditions.

Core Concepts:

Energy Equation over a hump: \(E_1 = E_2 + \Delta Z\)

For critical flow to just occur at the hump without affecting upstream: \(E_2 = E_c\), so \(\Delta Z_{max} = E_1 - E_c\).

Critical conditions (rectangular channel):

\[y_c = \left(\dfrac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3}, \quad E_c = 1.5\, y_c \]

Solution:

  1. Upstream Specific Energy \(E_1\):
    \(V_1 = \dfrac{10}{5 \times 1.5} = 1.333\) m/s
    \[E_1 = 1.5 + \dfrac{1.333^2}{2 \times 9.81} = 1.5 + 0.0906 = 1.5906 \text{ m} \]
  2. Critical Specific Energy \(E_c\):
    \(q = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2\) m²/s
    \[y_c = \left(\dfrac{4}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = (0.4077)^{1/3} = 0.7415 \text{ m} \]
    \[E_c = 1.5 \times 0.7415 = 1.112 \text{ m} \]
  3. Required hump height:
    \[\Delta Z = E_1 - E_c = 1.5906 - 1.112 = 0.4786 \text{ m} \approx 0.48 \text{ m} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.48 m | Acceptable Range: 0.45 to 0.51

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q16
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A hydraulic jump occurs in an open channel when the slope of the channel changes from _______.
options: STEEP slope to a STEEPER slope

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: STEEP slope to a STEEPER slope
structuredOptions.html: STEEP slope to a STEEPER slope

questions.explanation:
Hydraulics & Hydraulic Machines | Open Channel Flow (Hydraulic Jump)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data: Open channel with a change in bed slope.
  • Aim: Identify the condition for occurrence of a hydraulic jump.

Core Concepts:

Froude number: \(Fr = \dfrac{v}{\sqrt{g\,y}}\)

  • Supercritical flow: \(Fr > 1\) (steep slope, \(S_0 > S_c\))
  • Subcritical flow: \(Fr < 1\) (mild slope, \(S_0 < S_c\))

A hydraulic jump occurs when flow transitions from supercritical to subcritical, dissipating energy at the slope break. The reverse transition (mild to steep) produces no jump — flow simply accelerates smoothly.

Solution:

  1. Steep slope → uniform supercritical flow (\(Fr > 1\)).
  2. Sudden change to mild slope → normal depth becomes subcritical → a hydraulic jump forms to match the downstream depth condition.
  3. Transition from mild to steep causes no jump (flow accelerates).
  4. Hence, hydraulic jump occurs at: Steep slope → Mild slope.

Final Answer:

STEEP slope to MILD slope | Option(s): B

questions.question: Pick one or more CORRECT statement(s) from the choices given below, in the context of upstream and downstream cut-offs provided below the concrete apron of weirs / barrages constructed across alluvial rivers.
options: Cut-offs are provided to increase the rate of flow over the weir / barrage.
Cut-offs are provided to increase the seepage length and prevent failure due to piping.
The bottom level of cut-offs mainly depends on the scour depth.
Cut-offs are provided to ensure occurrence of hydraulic jump within the stilling basin.

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: Cut-offs are provided to increase the rate of flow over the weir / barrage.

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: Cut-offs are provided to ensure occurrence of hydraulic jump within the stilling basin.

questions.explanation:
Irrigation Engineering | Hydraulic Structures (Weirs on Permeable Foundations)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension + Application
  • Aim: Identify correct functions of upstream/downstream cut-offs in weir design.

Core Concepts:

Cut-offs (sheet piles) serve two primary purposes per Khosla's theory (IS 6966):

  • They increase the seepage path length → reduce exit hydraulic gradient below the critical value → prevent piping/internal erosion.
  • Their depth is governed by scour (Lacey's or Khosla's formula) to anchor below the maximum scour level.

Cut-offs do not control: the flow rate over the weir (controlled by crest geometry and head) or the hydraulic jump (controlled by baffle blocks and apron slope).

Common pitfall: Confusing seepage control with energy dissipation functions.

Solution:

  1. Option (A): Rate of flow over weir is unaffected by cut-offs → incorrect.
  2. Option (B): Cut-offs increase seepage path length → reduce piping risk → correct.
  3. Option (C): Bottom level of cut-offs is set below the maximum scour depth → correct.
  4. Option (D): Hydraulic jump is ensured by stilling basin geometry, not cut-offs → incorrect.

Final Answer:

Options B and C | Option(s): B; C

Hydrology | Runoff & Hydrograph Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Aim: Identify the effect of lower drainage density on hydrograph shape (all else constant).

Core Concepts:

Drainage density \(D_d\) (km/km²) = Total stream length / Catchment area.

  • Higher \(D_d\): Shorter overland flow paths → faster concentration → higher peak discharge \(Q_p\), shorter time base \(T_b\).
  • Lower \(D_d\): Longer overland flow paths → slower concentration → lower \(Q_p\), longer \(T_b\).

Conceptual link: Time of concentration \(t_c \propto 1/\sqrt{D_d}\).

Common pitfall: Reversing the relationship between peak discharge and time base.

Solution:

  1. Option (B): Lower \(D_d\) → longer flow paths → attenuated (lower) peak discharge → correct.
  2. Option (C): Longer travel time → extended recession limb → longer time base \(T_b\) → correct.
  3. Options (A) & (D): Opposite of the correct behaviour → incorrect.

Final Answer:

Options B and C | Option(s): B; C

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q33
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Consider steady flow of water in the series pipe system shown below, with specified discharge. The diameters of Pipes A and B are 2 m and 1 m, respectively. The lengths of pipes A and B are 100 m and 200 m, respectively. Assume the Darcy-Weisbach friction coefficient, f as 0.01 for both the pipes.
The ratio of head loss in Pipe-B to the head loss in Pipe-A is _______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pipe Flow and Head Losses

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: \(D_A = 2~m\), \(L_A = 100~m\); \(D_B = 1~m\), \(L_B = 200~m\); friction factor \(f = 0.01\) (both pipes); series connection with identical discharge \(Q\).
  • Aim: Ratio of head loss in Pipe-B to head loss in Pipe-A, rounded to nearest integer.

Core Concepts:

Darcy-Weisbach formula:

\[h_f = \dfrac{f\,L\,V^2}{2\,g\,D}\]

Substituting velocity \(V = \dfrac{4Q}{\pi D^2}\) yields:

\[h_f = \dfrac{8\,f\,L\,Q^2}{\pi^2\,g\,D^5}\]

For the same \(Q\), \(f\), and \(g\): \(h_f \propto \dfrac{L}{D^5}\)

Therefore the head loss ratio is:

\[\dfrac{h_{fB}}{h_{fA}} = \dfrac{L_B}{L_A} \times \left(\dfrac{D_A}{D_B}\right)^5\]

Common pitfall: Using \(D^2\) instead of \(D^5\) in the ratio.

Solution:

  1. Length ratio: \(\dfrac{L_B}{L_A} = \dfrac{200}{100} = 2\)
  2. Diameter ratio: \(\dfrac{D_A}{D_B} = \dfrac{2}{1} = 2\)
  3. Raise to fifth power: \(2^5 = 32\)
  4. Head-loss ratio: \(2 \times 32 = 64\) (\(g\), \(f\), \(Q\), \(\pi\) cancel exactly)

Final Answer:

64

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Consider flow in a long and very wide rectangular open channel. Width of the channel can be considered as infinity compared to the depth of flow. Uniform flow depth is 1.0 m. The bed slope of the channel is 0.0001. The Manning roughness coefficient value is 0.02. Acceleration due to gravity, g can be taken as 9.81 m/s².
The critical depth (in m) corresponding to the flow rate resulting from the above conditions is _______ (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Open Channel Flow — Critical Depth

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Wide rectangular channel (\(B \to \infty\)), Uniform flow depth \(y_n = 1.0~m\), Bed slope \(S_0 = 0.0001\), Manning's roughness \(n = 0.02\), \(g = 9.81~m/s^2\).
  • Aim: Critical depth \(y_c\) in meters, rounded to one decimal place.

Core Concepts:

  • Wide channel approximation: Hydraulic radius \(R \approx y_n\).
  • Manning's Equation: \(V = \dfrac{1}{n}\,R^{2/3}\,S_0^{1/2}\)
  • Unit discharge: \(q = V \times y_n\)
  • Critical depth (rectangular channel): \(y_c = \left(\dfrac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3}\)

Solution:

  1. Hydraulic radius: \(R \approx y_n = 1.0~m\)
  2. Flow velocity:
    \[V = \dfrac{1}{0.02} \times (1.0)^{2/3} \times (0.0001)^{1/2} = 50 \times 1 \times 0.01 = 0.5~m/s\]
  3. Unit discharge: \(q = 0.5 \times 1.0 = 0.5~m^2/s\)
  4. Critical depth:
    \[y_c = \left(\dfrac{0.5^2}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\dfrac{0.25}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = (0.02548)^{1/3} \approx 0.294~m \approx \mathbf{0.3}~m\]

Final Answer:

0.3 m | Option(s): B

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The drag force, F_D on a sphere due to a fluid flowing past the sphere is a function of viscosity, μ, the mass density, ρ, the velocity of flow, V, and the diameter of the sphere, D.
Pick the relevant (one or more) non-dimensional parameter(s) pertaining to the above process from the following list.
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Dimensional Analysis (Buckingham π Theorem)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Drag force \(F_D\) is a function of viscosity \(\mu\), density \(\rho\), velocity \(V\), and diameter \(D\).
  • Aim: Identify relevant non-dimensional parameters.

Core Concepts:

  • Buckingham \(\pi\) Theorem: Groups \(n\) variables into \((n - m)\) non-dimensional \(\pi\) groups, where \(m\) = number of fundamental dimensions.
  • Drag Coefficient: \(C_D \propto \dfrac{F_D}{\rho V^2 D^2}\)
  • Reynolds Number: \(Re = \dfrac{\rho V D}{\mu}\)

Solution:

  1. Option (A) — \(\dfrac{F_D}{\rho V^2 D^2}\):
    \([F_D] = MLT^{-2}\)
    \([\rho V^2 D^2] = [ML^{-3}][L^2T^{-2}][L^2] = MLT^{-2}\)
    Result: \([M^0L^0T^0]\) → Non-dimensional (Drag Coefficient).
  2. Option (C) — \(\dfrac{\rho V D}{\mu}\):
    \([\rho V D] = [ML^{-3}][LT^{-1}][L] = ML^{-1}T^{-1}\)
    \([\mu] = ML^{-1}T^{-1}\)
    Result: \([M^0L^0T^0]\) → Non-dimensional (Reynolds Number).
  3. Options (B) and (D) do not yield dimensionless quantities or represent non-standard groupings → Incorrect.

Final Answer:

\(\dfrac{F_D}{\rho V^2 D^2}\) and \(\dfrac{\rho VD}{\mu}\) | Option(s): A and C

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q58
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A 60 cm diameter well completely penetrates a confined aquifer of permeability 5 × 10⁻⁴ m/s. The length of the strainer (spanning the entire thickness of the aquifer) is 10 m. The drawdown at the well under steady state pumping is 1.0 m. Assume that the radius of influence for this pumping is 300 m.
The discharge from the well (in litres per minute) is _______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Hydrology & Irrigation | Groundwater Hydraulics

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Well diameter \(= 60~cm \implies\) radius \(r_w = 0.3~m\), Permeability \(K = 5 \times 10^{-4}~m/s\), Strainer length (aquifer thickness) \(B = 10~m\), Steady state drawdown \(s_w = 1.0~m\), Radius of influence \(R = 300~m\).
  • Aim: Calculate the discharge from the well (\(Q\)) in liters per minute.

Core Concepts:

Thiem's Equation: Used for calculating the steady-state discharge of a fully penetrating well in a confined aquifer:

\[Q = \dfrac{2 \pi K B s_w}{\ln(R/r_w)}\]

Unit Conversions: Always track volumetric flow rate conversions meticulously (\(1~m^3 = 1000~litres\), \(1~minute = 60~seconds\)).

Pitfall to avoid: Forgetting to convert the diameter to radius, or messing up the final time/volume conversion.

Solution:

  1. Calculate Discharge (\(Q\)) in \(m^3/s\):
    \[Q = \dfrac{2 \times \pi \times (5 \times 10^{-4}) \times 10 \times 1.0}{\ln\left(\dfrac{300}{0.3}\right)}\]\[Q = \dfrac{0.01\pi}{\ln(1000)} = \dfrac{0.0314159}{6.9077} = 0.004548~m^3/s\]
  2. Convert to Litres per Minute:
    Convert \(m^3\) to litres: \(0.004548 \times 1000 = 4.548~L/s\)
    Convert seconds to minutes: \(4.548 \times 60 = 272.88~L/min\)
  3. Round to nearest integer: \(273~L/min\)

Final Answer:

273 L/min | Option(s): Official Key Range is 271 to 273

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q59
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The peak of flood hydrograph due to a 3-hour duration storm in a catchment is 180 m³/s. The total rainfall depth is 6.6 cm. It can be assumed that the average infiltration loss is 0.2 cm/h. There are no other losses. The base flow is constant at a value of 30 m³/s.
The peak value of the 3-hour unit hydrograph for this catchment (in m³/s) is _______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Unit Hydrograph

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Peak of flood hydrograph \(Q_{peak} = 180~m^{3}/s\), storm duration \(t = 3~h\), total rainfall depth \(P = 6.6~cm\), average infiltration loss \(\phi = 0.2~cm/h\), base flow \(Q_b = 30~m^{3}/s\). There are no other losses.
  • Aim: Find the peak value of the 3-hour unit hydrograph in \(m^{3}/s\).

Core Concepts:

Direct Runoff Hydrograph (DRH) Peak: Obtained by subtracting the base flow from the peak of the flood hydrograph.

Effective Rainfall (\(P_e\)): The portion of rainfall that contributes to direct runoff, calculated as Total Rainfall minus Losses.

Unit Hydrograph (UH) Peak: By principle of linearity, the peak of a UH is the peak of the DRH divided by the effective rainfall depth.

Solution:

  1. Calculate total infiltration loss over the storm duration:
    \[\text{Loss} = \phi \times t = 0.2~cm/h \times 3~h = 0.6~cm\]
  2. Calculate effective rainfall \((P_e)\):
    \[P_e = P - \text{Loss} = 6.6~cm - 0.6~cm = 6.0~cm\]
  3. Calculate the peak of the DRH:
    \[\text{DRH}_{peak} = Q_{peak} - Q_b = 180~m^{3}/s - 30~m^{3}/s = 150~m^{3}/s\]
  4. Calculate the peak of the 3-hour UH:
    \[\text{UH}_{peak} = \dfrac{\text{DRH}_{peak}}{P_e} = \dfrac{150~m^{3}/s}{6.0~cm} = 25~m^{3}/s/cm\]

Final Answer:

25

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q60
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The shaft of a 6 m wide gate in the figure will fail at a moment of 3924 kN.m about the hinge P. The maximum value of water depth h (in m) that the gate can hold is _______ (round off to the nearest integer).
Note:
Density of water = 1000 kg/m³
Acceleration due to gravity = 9.81 m/s²
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Hydrostatic Forces

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Gate width \(b = 6~m\), failure moment about hinge \(M = 3924~kN.m\), density of water \(\rho = 1000~kg/m^{3}\), \(g = 9.81~m/s^{2}\).
  • Aim: Determine the maximum water depth \(h\) in meters.

Correction Protocol:

Sanity Check & Issue: The problem diagram indicates a hinge 'P' with dimensions "4 m" and "3 m". Taking moments about a hinge located 4m above the bottom yields a maximum possible moment of roughly 2511 kN.m (which is physically incapable of reaching the 3924 kN.m failure threshold).

Correction: For the moment to reach 3924 kN.m and align with physical reality and the official key, the hinge 'P' must act at the bottom of the gate structure, with the hydrostatic pressure acting against the gate. We will proceed with the moment taken about the bottom.

Core Concepts:

Hydrostatic pressure varies linearly with depth: \(p = \rho g z\).

Moment of hydrostatic force about the base for a depth \(h\):
\[M = \int_0^h (\rho g (h-y) b)\, y\, dy = \dfrac{\rho g b h^3}{6}\]

Solution:

  1. Equate the theoretical moment equation to the given failure moment:
    \[M = \dfrac{\rho g b h^3}{6}\]
  2. Substitute known values, ensuring consistent units (converting \(3924~kN.m\) to \(N.m\)):
    \[3924 \times 10^3 = \dfrac{1000 \times 9.81 \times 6 \times h^3}{6}\]
  3. Simplify the equation:
    \[3924 \times 10^3 = 9810 \times h^3\]
  4. Solve for \(h^3\):
    \[h^3 = \dfrac{3924000}{9810} = 400\]
  5. Solve for \(h\):
    \[h = \sqrt[3]{400} \approx 7.368~m\]
    Rounding to the nearest integer gives 7, perfectly aligning with the answer key range.

Final Answer:

7

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 1 | CE Q20
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The number of degrees of freedom for a natural open channel flow with a mobile bed is
questions.explanation:
Hydraulics & Open Channel Flow | Mobile-Bed / Alluvial Channels

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: Natural open channel flow with a mobile (alluvial) bed.
  • Aim: Determine the number of degrees of freedom.

Core Concepts:

  • Rigid-boundary channel: Depth \(y\) is determined by the resistance law (Manning/Chezy) for given \(Q\), \(B\), \(S_0\) → 1–2 degrees of freedom.
  • Mobile-bed natural channel: The bed erodes and deposits freely, introducing additional independent variables: flow depth \(y\), channel width \(B\), longitudinal slope \(S_0\), and sediment transport rate/concentration → 4 degrees of freedom (regime theory: Lacey, Blench, etc.).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. For a rigid bed: \(Q\) given → \(y\) from Manning; \(S_0\) fixed → 1 DOF.
  2. For a mobile bed: the channel self-adjusts \(B\), \(y\), \(S_0\), and sediment load independently.
  3. Four independent variables can be varied freely while satisfying equilibrium conditions (continuity + resistance + sediment transport).
  4. Fluvial hydraulics literature confirms 4 degrees of freedom for natural alluvial channels.

Common Pitfall: Using the rigid-bed value of 2 or 3.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 4 | Option(s): C

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 1 | CE Q35
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A 30 cm diameter well fully penetrates an unconfined aquifer of saturated thickness 20 m with hydraulic conductivity of 10 m/day. Under the steady pumping rate for a long time, the drawdowns in two observation wells located at 10 m and 100 m from the pumping well are 5 m and 1 m, respectively. The corresponding pumping rate (in m³/day) from the well is ________________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Groundwater Hydrology / Well Hydraulics

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Well diameter = 30 cm (not used directly)
    • Aquifer thickness \(H = 20\) m
    • Hydraulic conductivity \(k = 10\) m/day
    • Drawdown \(s_1 = 5\) m at \(r_1 = 10\) m
    • Drawdown \(s_2 = 1\) m at \(r_2 = 100\) m
    • Steady state flow
  • Aim: Find pumping rate \(Q\) in m³/day.

Core Concepts:

Thiem's Equation (unconfined aquifer, steady radial flow):\[Q = \dfrac{\pi k (h_2^2 - h_1^2)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)}\]where \(h = H - s\) is the remaining saturated thickness.

Derived from Dupuit-Forchheimer assumptions integrating Darcy's law for fully penetrating well.

Common Pitfall: Using the confined aquifer formula \(Q = \dfrac{2\pi kH(h_2-h_1)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)}\); mixing up \(s\) and \(h\); incorrect order of \(\ln\) term.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Compute saturated thicknesses:\[h_1 = 20 - 5 = 15 \text{ m}, \quad h_2 = 20 - 1 = 19 \text{ m}\]

  2. Compute squares and difference:\[h_1^2 = 225 \text{ m}^2, \quad h_2^2 = 361 \text{ m}^2, \quad h_2^2 - h_1^2 = 136 \text{ m}^2\]

  3. Log term:\[\ln\left(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}\right) = \ln\left(\dfrac{100}{10}\right) = \ln(10) \approx 2.302585\]

  4. Pumping rate:\[Q = \dfrac{\pi \times 10 \times 136}{2.302585} = \dfrac{4272.96}{2.302585} \approx 1855.65 \text{ m}^3/\text{day}\]

Sanity check: \(Q \approx 1856\) m³/day is realistic for \(k = 10\) m/day with a significant drawdown cone; \(h_1 = 15 > 0\) confirms no aquifer dryout.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1855.65 m³/day

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 1 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A flow velocity field \( \vec{V}: \vec{V}(x,y) \) for a fluid is represented by

\[\vec{V} = 3 \hat{i} + (5x) \hat{j} \]

In the context of the fluid and the flow, which one of the following statements is CORRECT?
options: The fluid is incompressible and the flow is rotational.
The fluid is incompressible and the flow is irrotational.
The fluid is compressible and the flow is rotational.
The fluid is compressible and the flow is irrotational.

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: The fluid is incompressible and the flow is rotational.
structuredOptions.html: The fluid is incompressible and the flow is rotational.

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: The fluid is incompressible and the flow is irrotational.
structuredOptions.html: The fluid is incompressible and the flow is irrotational.

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: The fluid is compressible and the flow is rotational.
structuredOptions.html: The fluid is compressible and the flow is rotational.

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: The fluid is compressible and the flow is irrotational.
structuredOptions.html: The fluid is compressible and the flow is irrotational.

questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Kinematics of Flow

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Flow velocity vector \(\vec{V} = 3\hat{i} + (5x)\hat{j}\)
  • Aim: Determine if the fluid is compressible/incompressible and if the flow is rotational/irrotational.

Core Concepts:

Continuity Equation (Compressibility): A flow is incompressible if the divergence of the velocity vector is zero (\( abla \cdot \vec{V} = 0\)):\[\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y} = 0\]

Vorticity (Rotationality): A flow is irrotational if the curl of the velocity vector is zero. For 2D flow, rotationality depends on rotation about the z-axis:\[\omega_z = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} ight)\]

Solution Method:

  1. Extract velocity components \(u\) and \(v\) from the given vector.
  2. Apply the continuity equation to check for compressibility.
  3. Calculate the rotation component \(\omega_z\) to check for rotationality.

Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Identify Components: \(u = 3\) and \(v = 5x\)

Step 2: Check Compressibility:

\[ abla \cdot \vec{V} = \dfrac{\partial (3)}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial (5x)}{\partial y} = 0 + 0 = 0\]

Since the divergence is zero, the fluid flow is incompressible.

Step 3: Check Rotationality:

\[2\omega_z = \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial (5x)}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial (3)}{\partial y} = 5 - 0 = 5\]

Since the rotation component is not zero (\(5 eq 0\)), the flow is rotational.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: The fluid is incompressible and the flow is rotational | Option(s): A

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 1 | CE Q47
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The return period of a large earthquake for a given region is 200 years. Assuming that earthquake occurrence follows Poisson’s distribution, the probability that it will be exceeded at least once in 50 years is __________ % (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Flood Frequency Analysis

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Return period (\(T\)) = 200 years
    • Design life/Period (\(n\)) = 50 years
  • Aim: Find the probability of the event exceeding at least once in 50 years, assuming a Poisson distribution.

Core Concepts:

  • Probability of Occurrence (\(p\)): The annual exceedance probability is \(p = \dfrac{1}{T}\).
  • Poisson Distribution: Used for modeling discrete, rare events over time. The probability of exactly \(x\) occurrences in time \(t\) is \[P(x) = \dfrac{(\lambda t)^x e^{-\lambda t}}{x!}\] where \(\lambda\) is the average rate of occurrence per year.
  • Risk: The probability of at least one exceedance is \(P(x \ge 1) = 1 - P(x=0)\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Annual Rate (\(\lambda\)):\[\lambda = \dfrac{1}{200} = 0.005 \text{ events/year}\]

  2. Calculate Expected Events (\(\lambda t\)):\[\lambda t = 0.005 \times 50 = 0.25\]

  3. Apply Poisson Formula for Zero Occurrences:\[P(0) = \dfrac{(0.25)^0 e^{-0.25}}{0!} = e^{-0.25} \approx 0.7788\]

  4. Calculate Risk:\[\text{Risk} = 1 - 0.7788 = 0.2212\]

  5. Convert to Percentage:\[0.2212 \times 100\% = 22.12\% \approx 22\%\]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 22% | Option(s): NAT

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 1 | CE Q56
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The ordinates of a 1-hour unit hydrograph (UH) are given below.

Time (hours)012345
Ordinates of 1-hour UH (m³/s)01350809585
Time (hours)67891011
Ordinates of 1-hour UH (m³/s)5535151030

These ordinates are used to derive a 3-hour UH. The peak discharge (in m³/s) for the derived 3-hour UH is ____________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Unit Hydrograph Derivation

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Ordinates of a 1-hour Unit Hydrograph (UH) at 1-hour intervals.
  • Aim: Determine the peak discharge of a derived 3-hour UH.

Core Concepts:

Superposition Method: Since the desired duration (3 hours) is an integer multiple of the given duration (1 hour), the superposition method is the most efficient approach. The principle of linearity states that lagging the 1-hr UH by 1 hour and 2 hours, adding the ordinates, and dividing by 3 will yield the ordinates of the 3-hour UH.

Solution Method:

  1. List the 1-hr UH ordinates.
  2. Lag the ordinates by 1 hour and by 2 hours.
  3. Sum the three columns to get the ordinates of a Direct Runoff Hydrograph (DRH) for a 3-hour storm of 3 cm excess rainfall.
  4. Divide the summed ordinates by 3 to get the 3-hour UH ordinates.
  5. Identify the maximum value.

Step-by-Step Execution:

Time (hr)1-hr UH (U₁)Lagged 1-hr (U₂)Lagged 2-hr (U₃)Sum (U₁+U₂+U₃)3-hr UH (Sum/3)
00——00

The maximum ordinate of the derived 3-hour UH is 86.67 m³/s, which rounds to 87 m³/s.

Final Answer: 87 | Accepted key range: 86 to 88

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 1 | CE Q57
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A standard round bottom triangular canal section as shown in the figure has a bed slope of 1 in 200. Consider the Chezy’s coefficient as 150 m¹/²/s.




The normal depth of flow, \( y \) (in meters) for carrying a discharge of 20 m³/s is ____________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Open Channel Flow | Uniform Flow

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Standard round bottom triangular canal section
    • Bed slope \(S = 1/200\)
    • Chezy's coefficient \(C = 150\) m\(^{1/2}\)/s
    • Discharge \(Q = 20\) m³/s
  • Aim: Find the normal depth of flow \(y\) in meters.

Core Concepts:

Geometry: For the standard lined triangular section, the radius of the circular bottom equals \(y\) and the center of the arc lies at the free water surface. This gives a hydraulic radius that simplifies elegantly to \(R = y/2\).

Chezy's Equation: \(Q = C \cdot A \cdot \sqrt{R \cdot S}\)

Solution Method:

  1. Calculate angle \(\theta\): side slope has vertical = 1, horizontal = 1.5, so \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(1/1.5)\) (in radians).
  2. Determine area: \(A = y^2(\theta + \cot\theta)\).
  3. Determine hydraulic radius: \(R = y/2\).
  4. Substitute into Chezy's formula and solve for \(y\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Angle of normal:\[\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{1.5}\right) = 0.588 \text{ rad}, \quad \cot\theta = 1.5\]

  2. Area calculation:\[A = y^2(0.588 + 1.5) = 2.088\, y^2\]

  3. Chezy's application:\[20 = 150 \cdot (2.088\,y^2) \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{y}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{200}}\]\[20 = 313.2\,y^2 \cdot \dfrac{y^{0.5}}{20} = 15.66\, y^{2.5}\]\[y^{2.5} = \dfrac{20}{15.66} = 1.277\]\[y = (1.277)^{0.4} = 1.102 \text{ m}\]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.10 m | Accepted key range: 1.09 to 1.12

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 1 | CE Q58
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A spillway has unit discharge of 7.5 m³/s/m. The flow depth at the downstream horizontal apron is 0.5 m. The tail water depth (in meters) required to form a hydraulic jump is ____________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Open Channel Flow | Hydraulic Jump

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Unit discharge \(q = 7.5\) m³/s/m
    • Initial flow depth \(y_1 = 0.5\) m
  • Aim: Calculate the tailwater depth (\(y_2\)) required for a hydraulic jump.

Core Concepts:

Froude Number (\(Fr\)): Ratio of inertial forces to gravity forces. \(Fr_1 = V_1 / \sqrt{g \cdot y_1}\)

Belanger Equation: Relates conjugate depths in a horizontal rectangular channel.\[y_2 = \dfrac{y_1}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2} - 1\right)\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Initial Velocity:\[V_1 = \dfrac{q}{y_1} = \dfrac{7.5}{0.5} = 15 \text{ m/s}\]

  2. Froude Number Squared:\[Fr_1^2 = \dfrac{V_1^2}{g \cdot y_1} = \dfrac{225}{9.81 \times 0.5} = \dfrac{225}{4.905} = 45.87\]

  3. Belanger Equation:\[y_2 = \dfrac{0.5}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8(45.87)} - 1\right) = 0.25\left(\sqrt{367.96} - 1\right)\]\[y_2 = 0.25(19.182 - 1) = 0.25 \times 18.182 = 4.545 \text{ m}\]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 4.55 m | Accepted key range: 4.40 to 4.70

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 1 | CE Q59
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A 5 m × 5 m closed tank of 10 m height contains water and oil, and is connected to an overhead water reservoir as shown in the figure. Use \( \gamma_w = 10 \text{ kN/m}^3 \) and Specific gravity of oil = 0.8.




The total force (in kN) due to pressure on the side PQR of the tank is ______________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Hydrostatic Forces

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Right tank: 5 m × 5 m base, closed top, 10 m height; connected to an overhead water reservoir
    • \(\gamma_w = 10\) kN/m³; Specific gravity of oil = 0.8, so \(\gamma_{oil} = 8\) kN/m³
  • Aim: Find the total hydrostatic pressure force on the face PQR.

Core Concepts:

  • Manometry & Pressure Transmission: Pressure from the left open tank transfers directly to the right closed tank via the connecting pipe.
  • Hydrostatic Pressure Distribution: Pressure increases linearly with depth (\(P = P_0 + \gamma \cdot h\)).
  • Force Calculation: Total force = area under the pressure diagram × width of the face.

Solution Method:

Pitfall Warning: Visual diagram interpretation is critical. Key geometry: the connecting pipe steps down 2m; the top pipe is 8m below the left free surface; oil layer thickness = 4m (R to Q); water layer thickness = 6m (Q to P); the pipe connects at interface Q.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Depth to Interface Q:\[\text{Depth to Q} = 8 + 2 = 10 \text{ m}\]

  2. Pressure at Q:\[P_Q = \gamma_w \cdot h = 10 \times 10 = 100 \text{ kPa}\]

  3. Pressure at Top (R) — moving up through oil:\[P_R = P_Q - \gamma_{oil} \cdot h_{oil} = 100 - (8 \times 4) = 68 \text{ kPa}\]

  4. Pressure at Bottom (P) — moving down through water:\[P_P = P_Q + \gamma_w \cdot h_{water} = 100 + (10 \times 6) = 160 \text{ kPa}\]

  5. Force on oil zone (R to Q), width = 5 m:\[F_{oil} = \dfrac{P_R + P_Q}{2} \cdot h_{oil} \cdot B = \dfrac{68 + 100}{2} \times 4 \times 5 = 84 \times 20 = 1680 \text{ kN}\]

  6. Force on water zone (Q to P), width = 5 m:\[F_{water} = \dfrac{P_Q + P_P}{2} \cdot h_{water} \cdot B = \dfrac{100 + 160}{2} \times 6 \times 5 = 130 \times 30 = 3900 \text{ kN}\]

  7. Total Force:\[F_{total} = 1680 + 3900 = 5580 \text{ kN}\]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 5580 kN | Accepted key range: 5575 to 5585
