questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Rheology of Fluids (Viscosity Models)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Plot of shear stress (\(\tau\)) vs velocity gradient (\(du/dy\)) for materials/fluids P, Q, R, S, T.
  • Aim: Identify correct matching of material/fluid types.

Core Concepts:

  • Real solid: Vertical line (\(\tau\) finite at \(du/dy = 0\))
  • Ideal Bingham plastic: \(\tau = \tau_0 + \mu(du/dy)\) → yield stress intercept then linear
  • Newtonian fluid: \(\tau = \mu(du/dy)\) → straight line through origin
  • Ideal fluid: \(\tau = 0\) → horizontal line at \(\tau = 0\)
  • Non-Newtonian: Curved line

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. P: Vertical line (stress without flow) → Real solid
  2. Q: Yield stress intercept then linear → Ideal Bingham plastic
  3. S: Straight line through origin → Newtonian fluid
  4. T: Horizontal line (\(\tau = 0\)) → Ideal fluid

Final Answer:

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q35
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A 2 m wide rectangular channel is carrying a discharge of 30 m³/s at a bed slope of 1 in 300. Assuming the energy correction factor as 1.1 and acceleration due to gravity as 10 m/s², the critical depth of flow (in meters) is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow (Critical Depth with Energy Correction)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Rectangular channel width \(B = 2\text{ m}\), discharge \(Q = 30\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\), energy correction factor \(\alpha = 1.1\), \(g = 10\text{ m/s}^2\).
  • Aim: Critical depth \(y_c\) (m, rounded to 2 decimal places).

Core Concepts:

Critical flow condition (\(dE/dy = 0\)) with energy correction factor \(\alpha\):
\[\alpha \dfrac{Q^2 B}{g A^3} = 1 \]
For a rectangular channel this simplifies to:
\[y_c = \left(\dfrac{\alpha Q^2}{g B^2}\right)^{1/3} \]
Note: Omitting \(\alpha\) is a common pitfall.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. \[\alpha Q^2 = 1.1 \times 30^2 = 1.1 \times 900 = 990 \]
  2. \[g B^2 = 10 \times 2^2 = 40 \]
  3. \[\dfrac{\alpha Q^2}{g B^2} = \dfrac{990}{40} = 24.75 \]
  4. \[y_c = (24.75)^{1/3} \approx 2.91\text{ m} \]
    (Verification: \(2.914^3 \approx 24.75\) ✓)
  5. Without \(\alpha\), \(y_c \approx 2.88\text{ m}\); \(\alpha > 1\) increases \(y_c\) as expected.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2.91 m | Accepted range: [2.88 to 2.94]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A round-bottom triangular lined canal is to be laid at a slope of 1 in 1500, to carry a discharge of 25 m³/s. The side slopes of the canal cross-section are to be kept at 1.25H : 1V. If Manning’s roughness coefficient is 0.013, the flow depth (in meters) will be in the range of
questions.explanation:
Open Channel Flow | Lined Canals

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Discharge, \(Q = 25\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
    Bed slope, \(S = 1/1500\)
    Side slopes, \(m = 1.25\text{ (H)} : 1\text{ (V)}\)
    Manning's roughness, \(n = 0.013\)
    Section: Round-bottom triangular lined canal
  • Aim: Determine the normal flow depth, \(y\) (in meters).

Core Concepts:

According to IS 10430 (Criteria for Design of Lined Canals), a round-bottom triangular canal is designed such that the circular arc at the bed is tangential to the straight side slopes, and its center lies at the water surface. This geometry forms the "best hydraulic section" for a triangle.

Let \(\theta\) be the angle the side slope makes with the vertical (in radians): \(\tan\theta = \text{Horizontal} / \text{Vertical} = m = 1.25\)

  • Cross-sectional Area: \(A = y^2(\theta + \tan\theta)\)
  • Wetted Perimeter: \(P = 2y(\theta + \tan\theta)\)
  • Hydraulic Radius: \(R = A/P = y/2\)
  • Manning's Equation: \(Q = \dfrac{1}{n} A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate the angle \(\theta\):
    \[\tan\theta = 1.25 \Rightarrow \theta = \arctan(1.25) = 0.8961\text{ radians} \]
  2. Express Area and Perimeter in terms of \(y\):
    Geometric constant \(k = (\theta + \tan\theta) = 0.8961 + 1.25 = 2.1461\)
    \[A = 2.1461\, y^2, \quad R = y/2 = 0.5y \]
  3. Apply Manning's Equation:
    \[25 = \dfrac{1}{0.013} \times (2.1461\, y^2) \times (0.5y)^{2/3} \times \left(\dfrac{1}{1500}\right)^{1/2} \]\[25 = 76.923 \times 2.1461 \times 0.630\, y^{2/3} \times 0.02582\, y^2 \]\[25 = 2.684\, y^{8/3} \]
  4. Solve for \(y\):
    \[y^{8/3} = \dfrac{25}{2.684} = 9.314 \]\[y = (9.314)^{3/8} = 2.404\text{ m} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(y \approx 2.40\text{ m}\) | Accepted key range: [2.39 to 2.42]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q56
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A storm with a recorded precipitation of 11.0 cm, as shown in the table, produced a direct run-off of 6.0 cm.

Time from start (hours)12345678
Recorded cumulative precipitation (cm)0.51.53.15.57.38.910.211.0

The \( \phi \)-index of this storm is _________ cm/hr (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Precipitation and Runoff

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Total precipitation = 11.0 cm
    Direct runoff = 6.0 cm
    Cumulative rainfall table over 8 hours
  • Aim: Calculate the \(\phi\)-index.

Core Concepts:

\(\phi\)-index: The average rainfall intensity above which the volume of rainfall equals the volume of runoff. It is an iterative calculation — any hours with rainfall intensity less than the assumed \(\phi\)-index do not contribute to runoff and must be excluded from the effective time calculation.

Solution Method:

Convert cumulative rainfall into hourly increments. Calculate initial average infiltration (W-index). Use this as a first trial for \(\phi\). Exclude hours where rainfall < trial \(\phi\), recalculate, and verify.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Extract Hourly Precipitation (\(P_i\) in cm/hr):
    • Hour 1: 0.5 cm
    • Hour 2: 1.5 − 0.5 = 1.0 cm
    • Hour 3: 3.1 − 1.5 = 1.6 cm
    • Hour 4: 5.5 − 3.1 = 2.4 cm
    • Hour 5: 7.3 − 5.5 = 1.8 cm
    • Hour 6: 8.9 − 7.3 = 1.6 cm
    • Hour 7: 10.2 − 8.9 = 1.3 cm
    • Hour 8: 11.0 − 10.2 = 0.8 cm
  2. Trial 1 — W-index approximation:
    \[W_{index} = \dfrac{11.0 - 6.0}{8} = 0.625\text{ cm/hr} \]
    Check: Hour 1 rainfall (0.5 cm) < 0.625 cm/hr → produces no runoff and must be excluded.
  3. Trial 2 — Refined \(\phi\):
    Effective Time \(t_e = 8 - 1 = 7\) hours
    Effective Precipitation \(P_e = 11.0 - 0.5 = 10.5\) cm
    \[\phi = \dfrac{P_e - \text{Runoff}}{t_e} = \dfrac{10.5 - 6.0}{7} = \dfrac{4.5}{7} \approx 0.6428\text{ cm/hr} \]
  4. Final Verification: All remaining 7 hours have rainfall ≥ 0.6428 cm/hr (minimum is hour 8 at 0.8 cm/hr). The assumption holds. ✓

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\phi = 0.64\text{ cm/hr}\) | Accepted key range: [0.64 to 0.65]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q57
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A 500 m long water distribution pipeline P with diameter 1.0 m, is used to convey 0.1 m³/s of flow. A new pipeline Q, with the same length and flow rate, is to replace P. The friction factors for P and Q are 0.04 and 0.01, respectively. The diameter of the pipeline Q (in meters) is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pipe Flow

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Pipeline P: \(L = 500\text{ m}\), \(D_P = 1.0\text{ m}\), \(Q = 0.1\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\), \(f_P = 0.04\)
    Pipeline Q: Same \(L\) and \(Q\), \(f_Q = 0.01\)
  • Aim: Find the required diameter of pipeline Q (\(D_Q\)) to functionally replace P.

Core Concepts:

Hydraulic Equivalence: When a pipe replaces another carrying the same flow, it must induce the exact same head loss so the system hydraulics remain balanced.

Darcy-Weisbach Equation: \(h_f = \dfrac{fLQ^2}{12.1\,D^5}\)

Solution Method:

Equate the head loss equations for both pipes. Since \(L\) and \(Q\) are constant, they cancel out, leaving a direct relationship between friction factors and diameters.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Equate Head Losses:
    \[h_{f,P} = h_{f,Q} \implies \dfrac{f_P L Q^2}{12.1\,D_P^5} = \dfrac{f_Q L Q^2}{12.1\,D_Q^5} \]
  2. Simplify and Solve:
    \[\dfrac{f_P}{D_P^5} = \dfrac{f_Q}{D_Q^5} \implies \dfrac{0.04}{1.0^5} = \dfrac{0.01}{D_Q^5} \]\[D_Q^5 = \dfrac{0.01}{0.04} = 0.25 \]\[D_Q = (0.25)^{1/5} \approx 0.7578\text{ m} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(D_Q \approx 0.76\text{ m}\) | Accepted key range: [0.70 to 0.80]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q58
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A 2 m × 1.5 m tank of 6 m height is provided with a 100 mm diameter orifice at the center of its base. The orifice is plugged and the tank is filled up to 5 m height. Consider the average value of discharge coefficient as 0.6 and acceleration due to gravity (\( g \)) as 10 m/s². After unplugging the orifice, the time (in seconds) taken for the water level to drop from 5 m to 3.5 m under free discharge condition is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Orifice Discharge

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Tank area (\(A\)) \(= 2 \times 1.5 = 3.0\text{ m}^2\)
    Orifice diameter (\(d\)) = 100 mm = 0.1 m
    Initial head (\(h_1\)) = 5 m
    Final head (\(h_2\)) = 3.5 m
    Discharge coefficient (\(C_d\)) = 0.6
    Gravity (\(g\)) = 10 m/s²
  • Aim: Calculate the time taken for the water level to drop from \(h_1\) to \(h_2\).

Core Concepts:

Tank Emptying Equation: Derived by equating the volumetric drop in the tank to the volumetric flow rate through the orifice over time \(dt\):

\[t = \dfrac{2A}{C_d \cdot a \cdot \sqrt{2g}} \left(\sqrt{h_1} - \sqrt{h_2}\right) \]

Solution Method:

Calculate the cross-sectional area of the orifice, then apply the standard tank emptying integral formula directly. Ensure unit consistency (orifice diameter in meters).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Orifice Area (\(a\)):
    \[a = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.1)^2 = 0.007854\text{ m}^2 \]
  2. Apply the Emptying Formula:
    \[t = \dfrac{2 \times 3.0}{0.6 \times 0.007854 \times \sqrt{2 \times 10}} \left(\sqrt{5} - \sqrt{3.5}\right) \]\[t = \dfrac{6.0}{0.0047124 \times 4.4721} \times (2.2360 - 1.8708) \]\[t = \dfrac{6.0}{0.021074} \times 0.3652 \]\[t = 284.71 \times 0.3652 \approx 103.98\text{ seconds} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 103.98 seconds | Accepted key range: [102.00 to 106.00]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q59
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A rectangular channel is 4.0 m wide and carries a discharge of 2.0 m³/s with a depth of 0.4 m. The channel transitions to a maximum width contraction at a downstream location, without influencing the upstream flow conditions. The width (in meters) at the maximum contraction is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow (Specific Energy)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Rectangular channel, initial width (\(B_1\)) = 4.0 m
    Discharge (\(Q\)) = 2.0 m³/s
    Initial depth (\(y_1\)) = 0.4 m
    Transition to maximum width contraction without altering upstream flow.
  • Aim: Find the width at the maximum contraction (\(B_2\)).

Core Concepts:

  • Specific Energy (\(E\)): Energy per unit weight of water relative to the channel bottom: \(E = y + \dfrac{V^2}{2g}\)
  • Choking Condition: For maximum contraction without upstream influence, the specific energy at the contracted section (\(E_2\)) must equal the upstream specific energy (\(E_1\)), and flow at the contraction must just reach the critical state.
  • Critical Flow Relations (Rectangular Channel): \(E_c = 1.5\,y_c\)   and   \(y_c = \left(\dfrac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3}\), where \(q = Q/B_2\)

Solution Method:

Calculate the specific energy at section 1. Equate to the minimum specific energy required for critical flow at section 2. Back-calculate the critical depth (\(y_c\)), the unit discharge (\(q_2\)), and finally the contracted width (\(B_2\)).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Upstream Velocity (\(V_1\)):
    \[V_1 = \dfrac{Q}{B_1 \cdot y_1} = \dfrac{2.0}{4.0 \times 0.4} = 1.25\text{ m/s} \]
  2. Calculate Upstream Specific Energy (\(E_1\)):
    \[E_1 = y_1 + \dfrac{V_1^2}{2g} = 0.4 + \dfrac{1.25^2}{2 \times 9.81} = 0.4 + 0.0796 = 0.4796\text{ m} \]
  3. Apply Choking Condition (\(E_1 = E_c\)):
    \[E_c = 1.5\,y_c \implies 0.4796 = 1.5\,y_c \implies y_c = 0.3197\text{ m} \]
  4. Determine Maximum Unit Discharge (\(q_2\)):
    \[y_c^3 = \dfrac{q_2^2}{g} \implies q_2 = \sqrt{g \cdot y_c^3} = \sqrt{9.81 \times (0.3197)^3} = \sqrt{0.3206} = 0.5662\text{ m}^3\text{/s/m} \]
  5. Calculate Contracted Width (\(B_2\)):
    \[B_2 = \dfrac{Q}{q_2} = \dfrac{2.0}{0.5662} = 3.532\text{ m} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.53 m | Accepted key range: [3.45 to 3.65]

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q19
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: When a supercritical stream enters a mild-sloped (M) channel section, the type of flow profile would become _______.
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics & Hydraulics | Open Channel Flow

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Incoming stream: Supercritical flow \((F_r > 1,\; y < y_c)\)
    • Channel slope: Mild (M)
    • Mild slope definition: Normal depth \(y_n\) is greater than critical depth \(y_c\) \((y_n > y_c)\)
  • Aim: Identify the water surface profile.

Core Concepts:

Classification of Surface Profiles on Mild Slope:

  • Zone 1 \((y > y_n)\): Backwater curve — M1 profile
  • Zone 2 \((y_n > y > y_c)\): Drawdown curve — M2 profile
  • Zone 3 \((y < y_c < y_n)\): Rising curve — M3 profile

Dynamic equation for surface profiles:\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{S_0 - S_f}{1 - F_r^2} \]

Solution Method:

  1. Determine the relative position of the incoming flow depth with respect to \(y_n\) and \(y_c\).
  2. Identify the zone.
  3. Determine profile behavior (increasing/decreasing depth).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Compare Depths:
    • Mild slope \(\Rightarrow y_n > y_c\)
    • Supercritical flow \(\Rightarrow y_{\text{incoming}} < y_c\)
    • Therefore: \(y < y_c < y_n\) → Zone 3
  2. Identify Profile Type:
    On a Mild slope in Zone 3, the profile is designated as M3.
  3. Verify Profile Behavior:
    • \(y < y_c \Rightarrow F_r > 1 \Rightarrow 1 - F_r^2 < 0\) (Denominator negative)
    • \(y < y_n \Rightarrow\) Velocity is high \(\Rightarrow S_f > S_0\) (Numerator negative)
    • \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{(-)}{(-)} = +\) → Depth increases in the flow direction.
    The M3 profile is a rising curve (supercritical flow transitioning toward normal depth on a mild slope).

Final Answer:

M3 | Correct Option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q33
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A canal supplies water to an area growing wheat over 100 hectares. The duration between the first and last watering is 120 days, and the total depth of water required by the crop is 35 cm. The most intense watering is required over a period of 30 days and requires a total depth of water equal to 12 cm. Assuming precipitation to be negligible and neglecting all losses, the minimum discharge (in m³/s, rounded off to three decimal places) in the canal to satisfy the crop requirement is ________________.
questions.explanation:
Irrigation Engineering | Water Requirements of Crops

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Crop: Wheat; Area: \(A = 100\text{ ha}\)
    • Base period: \(B = 120\text{ days}\); Total depth: \(\Delta = 35\text{ cm}\)
    • Kor period: \(T_{kor} = 30\text{ days}\); Kor depth: \(\Delta_{kor} = 12\text{ cm}\)
    • Neglect precipitation and losses.
  • Aim: Minimum discharge \((Q)\) in the canal (m³/s).

Core Concepts:

The canal must supply the Kor depth during the Kor period — this peak demand governs the design discharge:

Average demand rate: \(\dfrac{0.35}{120} \approx 0.00292\text{ m/day}\)
Kor demand rate: \(\dfrac{0.12}{30} = 0.004\text{ m/day}\)
Since Kor demand \(>\) average demand, Kor governs.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Volume to be supplied during Kor period:\[\text{Volume} = 100\text{ ha} \times 0.12\text{ m} = 100 \times 10^4 \times 0.12 = 120{,}000\text{ m}^3 \]
  2. Convert Kor period to seconds:\[T = 30 \times 24 \times 3600 = 2{,}592{,}000\text{ s} \]
  3. Calculate discharge:\[Q = \dfrac{120{,}000}{2{,}592{,}000} \approx 0.046296\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \approx 0.046\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]

Final Answer:

\(Q \approx 0.046\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) | Accepted range: 0.045 to 0.047

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The ordinates of a one-hour unit hydrograph for a catchment are given below:

t (hour)01234567
Q (m³/s)09211812520


Using the principle of superposition, a D-hour unit hydrograph for the catchment was derived from this one-hour unit hydrograph. The ordinates of the D-hour unit hydrograph were obtained as 3 m³/s at t = 1 hour and 10 m³/s at t = 2 hour. The value of D (in integer) is ___________.
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Unit Hydrograph – Duration Derivation

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • 1-hour Unit Hydrograph (1-h UH) ordinates given
    • Derived D-hour UH ordinates: \(3\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) at \(t=1\text{ hr}\), \(10\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) at \(t=2\text{ hr}\)
  • Aim: Find the integer duration \(D\).

Core Concepts:

Superposition Principle:\[UH_D(t) = \dfrac{1}{D}\sum_{i=0}^{D-1} UH_1(t-i) \]A D-hour UH is the average of \(D\) lagged 1-hour UHs.

1-hour UH Ordinates:

Time (hr)01234567
\(UH_1\) (m³/s)09211812520

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Test \(D = 3\):\[UH_3(t) = \dfrac{UH_1(t) + UH_1(t-1) + UH_1(t-2)}{3} \]
  2. At \(t = 1\text{ hr}\):\[UH_3(1) = \dfrac{UH_1(1) + UH_1(0) + UH_1(-1)}{3} = \dfrac{9 + 0 + 0}{3} = 3\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \checkmark \]
  3. At \(t = 2\text{ hr}\):\[UH_3(2) = \dfrac{UH_1(2) + UH_1(1) + UH_1(0)}{3} = \dfrac{21 + 9 + 0}{3} = \dfrac{30}{3} = 10\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \checkmark \]
  4. Both values match perfectly for \(D = 3\).

Final Answer:

\(D = 3\text{ hours}\) | Accepted range: 3 to 3

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A very wide rectangular channel carries a discharge (Q) of 70 m³/s per meter width. Its bed slope changes from 0.0001 to 0.0009 at a point P, as shown in the figure (not to scale). The Manning's roughness coefficient of the channel is 0.01. What water surface profile(s) exist(s) near the point P?
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Open Channel Flow

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Discharge per unit width: \(q = 70\text{ m}^3/\text{s/m}\)
    • Initial bed slope: \(S_{01} = 0.0001\)
    • Final bed slope: \(S_{02} = 0.0009\)
    • Manning's roughness: \(n = 0.01\)
    • Channel: Very wide rectangular
  • Aim: Identify the water surface profiles upstream and downstream near slope transition point P.

Core Concepts:

  • Critical Depth: \(y_c = \left(\dfrac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3}\)
  • Normal Depth (wide rectangular channel, \(R \approx y\)):\[q = \dfrac{1}{n}\, y_n^{5/3}\, S_0^{1/2} \]
  • Slope Classification: Mild (M): \(y_n > y_c\)  |  Steep (S): \(y_n < y_c\)
  • Profile Zones: Zone 2 on Mild slope → M2 (drawdown); Zone 2 on Steep slope → S2 (drawdown)
  • Control Section: At a Mild→Steep transition, flow passes through critical depth at point P.

Common Pitfall: Assuming a hydraulic jump occurs. A hydraulic jump only occurs at Steep→Mild transitions, not Mild→Steep.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Critical Depth \((y_c)\):\[y_c = \left(\dfrac{70^2}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\dfrac{4900}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = (499.49)^{1/3} \approx 7.93\text{ m} \]
  2. Calculate Normal Depth for Slope 1 \((y_{n1})\):\[70 = \dfrac{1}{0.01} \times y_{n1}^{5/3} \times \sqrt{0.0001} = 100 \times y_{n1}^{5/3} \times 0.01 \]\[y_{n1}^{5/3} = 70 \Rightarrow y_{n1} = 70^{0.6} \approx 12.78\text{ m} \]Since \(y_{n1}\,(12.78\text{ m}) > y_c\,(7.93\text{ m})\) → Slope 1 is Mild (M).
  3. Calculate Normal Depth for Slope 2 \((y_{n2})\):\[70 = 100 \times y_{n2}^{5/3} \times \sqrt{0.0009} = 100 \times y_{n2}^{5/3} \times 0.03 \]\[y_{n2}^{5/3} = \dfrac{70}{3} = 23.33 \Rightarrow y_{n2} = (23.33)^{0.6} \approx 6.64\text{ m} \]Since \(y_{n2}\,(6.64\text{ m}) < y_c\,(7.93\text{ m})\) → Slope 2 is Steep (S).
  4. Identify Profiles:
    Point P is the control section where depth \(= y_c = 7.93\text{ m}\).
    • Upstream of P: Depth transitions from \(y_{n1}\,(12.78\text{ m})\) down to \(y_c\,(7.93\text{ m})\). Depth lies between \(y_{n1}\) and \(y_c\) → Zone 2 on Mild slope → M2 profile (drawdown curve).
    • Downstream of P: Depth transitions from \(y_c\,(7.93\text{ m})\) down to \(y_{n2}\,(6.64\text{ m})\). Depth lies between \(y_c\) and \(y_{n2}\) → Zone 2 on Steep slope → S2 profile (drawdown curve).

Final Answer:

M2 and S2 | Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q44
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A jet of water having a velocity of 20 m/s strikes a series of plates fixed radially on a wheel revolving in the same direction as the jet at 15 m/s. What is the percentage efficiency of the plates? (round off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Impact of Jets & Hydraulic Machines

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Velocity of water jet: \(V = 20\text{ m/s}\)
    • Velocity of moving radial plates (wheel): \(u = 15\text{ m/s}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the percentage efficiency of the plates.

Core Concepts:

  • Series of Plates: For a wheel with a series of continuous plates, the entire jet mass strikes the plates per second: \(\dot{m} = \rho A V\).
  • Force on plates: \(F_x = \rho A V (V - u)\)
  • Power Output: \(P_{out} = F_x \times u = \rho A V (V-u)\, u\)
  • Power Input (KE of jet): \(P_{in} = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho A V^3\)
  • Efficiency:\[\eta = \dfrac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} = \dfrac{2u(V-u)}{V^2} \]

Common Pitfall: Using the single moving plate formula \(\eta = \dfrac{2u(V-u)^2}{V^3}\) → gives incorrect \(6.25\%\). The keyword here is "series of plates fixed radially on a wheel".

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Apply the efficiency formula:\[\eta = \dfrac{2 \times u \times (V - u)}{V^2} \]
  2. Substitute values:\[\eta = \dfrac{2 \times 15 \times (20 - 15)}{20^2} = \dfrac{2 \times 15 \times 5}{400} = \dfrac{150}{400} = 0.375 \]
  3. Convert to percentage:\[\eta = 0.375 \times 100 = 37.5\% \]

Final Answer:

37.5% | Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q59
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A 12-hour storm occurs over a catchment and results in a direct runoff depth of 100 mm. The time-distribution of the rainfall intensity is shown in the figure (not to scale). The φ-index of the storm is (in mm, rounded off to two decimal places) ________________.
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Infiltration Indices – \(\phi\)-Index Calculation

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Duration: 12 hours; Direct Runoff: \(R = 100\text{ mm}\)
    • Rainfall hyetograph (trapezoidal): vertices at \((0,0)\), \((4,20)\), \((6,20)\), \((12,0)\) — time (hr) vs. intensity (mm/hr)
  • Aim: Calculate the \(\phi\)-index (mm/hr).

Core Concepts:

  • Mass Balance: Total Rainfall \((P)\) − Total Infiltration \((F)\) = Runoff \((R)\)
  • \(\phi\)-index: The constant intensity threshold above which rainfall volume equals runoff volume.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Total Rainfall \((P)\):
    Area of trapezoid with parallel sides 12 and 2 hrs, height 20 mm/hr:\[P = \dfrac{1}{2}(12 + 2) \times 20 = 140\text{ mm} \]
  2. Total Infiltration:\[W = P - R = 140 - 100 = 40\text{ mm} \]
  3. Define widths of runoff trapezoid above \(I = \phi\):
    • Rising limb: slope \(= 20/4 = 5\) → time \(t_1 = \phi/5 = 0.2\phi\)
    • Falling limb: \(I = 20 - \dfrac{10}{3}(t-6)\) → time \(t_2 = 12 - 0.3\phi\)
    • Bottom width of runoff trapezoid: \(w_\phi = t_2 - t_1 = 12 - 0.5\phi\)
    • Top width (flat peak): \(= 6 - 4 = 2\text{ hrs}\)
  4. Runoff area equation:\[R = \dfrac{1}{2}(2 + 12 - 0.5\phi)(20 - \phi) \]\[200 = (14 - 0.5\phi)(20 - \phi) \]\[200 = 280 - 14\phi - 10\phi + 0.5\phi^2 \]\[0.5\phi^2 - 24\phi + 80 = 0 \Rightarrow \phi^2 - 48\phi + 160 = 0 \]
  5. Solve the quadratic:\[\phi = \dfrac{48 \pm \sqrt{2304 - 640}}{2} = \dfrac{48 \pm \sqrt{1664}}{2} = \dfrac{48 \pm 40.79}{2} \]
    • Root 1: \(44.4\) mm/hr (rejected, \(> I_{\max} = 20\))
    • Root 2: \(\phi \approx 3.60\) mm/hr ✓

Note: Official key indicates MTA (Marks to All) due to potential data ambiguity, but 3.60 is the mathematically derived value.

Final Answer:

\(\phi \approx 3.60\text{ mm/hr}\)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q60
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A hydraulic jump occurs in a 1.0 m wide horizontal, frictionless, rectangular channel, with a pre-jump depth of 0.2 m and a post-jump depth of 1.0 m. The value of g may be taken as 10 m/s². The values of the specific force at the pre-jump and post-jump sections are same and are equal to (in m³, rounded off to two decimal places) ________________.
questions.explanation:
Water Resources | Open Channel Flow – Hydraulic Jump / Specific Force

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Rectangular channel width: \(B = 1.0\text{ m}\)
    • Pre-jump depth: \(y_1 = 0.2\text{ m}\)
    • Post-jump depth: \(y_2 = 1.0\text{ m}\)
    • \(g = 10\text{ m/s}^2\)
  • Aim: Specific force \((F)\) at the jump sections.

Core Concepts:

Specific Force (rectangular channel):\[F = \dfrac{Q^2}{gBy} + \dfrac{By^2}{2} \]

Sequent depth relation:\[\dfrac{y_2}{y_1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8\,Fr_1^2} - 1\right) \]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Find \(Fr_1^2\) from sequent depth ratio:\[\dfrac{1.0}{0.2} = 5 = \dfrac{1}{2}(\sqrt{1 + 8\,Fr_1^2} - 1) \]\[11 = \sqrt{1 + 8\,Fr_1^2} \Rightarrow 121 = 1 + 8\,Fr_1^2 \Rightarrow Fr_1^2 = 15 \]
  2. Determine \(Q^2\):\[Fr_1^2 = \dfrac{v_1^2}{g\,y_1} \Rightarrow v_1^2 = 15 \times 10 \times 0.2 = 30 \]\[Q = A_1 v_1 = (1.0 \times 0.2) \times \sqrt{30} \]\[Q^2 = (0.2)^2 \times 30 = 1.2\text{ m}^4/\text{s}^2 \]
  3. Calculate Specific Force at Section 1:\[F = \dfrac{Q^2}{g\,B\,y_1} + \dfrac{B\,y_1^2}{2} = \dfrac{1.2}{10 \times 1 \times 0.2} + \dfrac{1 \times (0.2)^2}{2} \]\[F = 0.6 + 0.02 = 0.62\text{ m}^3 \]

Final Answer:

\(F = 0.62\text{ m}^3\) | Accepted range: 0.60 to 0.64

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q61
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: In Horton’s equation fitted to the infiltration data for a soil, the initial infiltration capacity is 10 mm/h; final infiltration capacity is 5 mm/h; and the exponential decay constant is 0.5 /h. Assuming that the infiltration takes place at capacity rates, the total infiltration depth (in mm) from a uniform storm of duration 12 h is ________________. (round off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Infiltration – Horton's Equation

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Initial capacity: \(f_0 = 10\text{ mm/h}\)
    • Final capacity: \(f_c = 5\text{ mm/h}\)
    • Decay constant: \(k = 0.5\text{ h}^{-1}\)
    • Duration: \(t = 12\text{ h}\)
  • Aim: Total infiltration depth \((F_p)\) in mm.

Core Concepts:

Horton's Equation:\[f(t) = f_c + (f_0 - f_c)\,e^{-kt} \]

Total Infiltration (integral of rate over time):\[F_p = \int_0^t f(t)\,dt = f_c\,t + \dfrac{f_0 - f_c}{k}(1 - e^{-kt}) \]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Substitute values:\[F_p = 5(12) + \dfrac{10 - 5}{0.5}(1 - e^{-0.5 \times 12}) \]
  2. Calculate each term:
    • Steady-state term: \(5 \times 12 = 60\text{ mm}\)
    • Transient coefficient: \(\dfrac{5}{0.5} = 10\text{ mm}\)
    • Exponential term: \(e^{-6} \approx 0.002479\)
  3. Final calculation:\[F_p = 60 + 10(1 - 0.002479) = 60 + 10(0.99752) \]\[F_p = 60 + 9.975 \approx 69.975\text{ mm} \approx 70.0\text{ mm} \]

Final Answer:

\(F_p \approx 70.0\text{ mm}\) | Accepted range: 69.7 to 70.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q20
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics

questions.explanation:

  • Aim: Identify the type of cross-drainage work from the structural configuration.

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q21

Which one of the following options provides the correct match of the terms listed in Column-1 and Column-2?

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q33
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The pressure in a pipe at X is to be measured by an open manometer as shown in figure. Fluid A is oil with a specific gravity of 0.8 and Fluid B is mercury with a specific gravity of 13.6. The absolute pressure at X is _________________ kN/m² (round off to one decimal place).
[Assume density of water as 1000 kg/m³ and acceleration due to gravity as 9.81 m/s² and atmospheric pressure as 101.3 kN/m²]
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pressure Measurement — Manometer

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Fluid A (oil): SG = 0.8, column height = 75 cm
    • Fluid B (mercury): SG = 13.6, column height = 25 cm
    • \(\rho_{water} = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3\), \(g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2\), \(P_{atm} = 101.3\text{ kN/m}^2\)
  • Aim: Absolute pressure at X (kN/m², one decimal).

2. Core Concepts:

Hydrostatic pressure balance in an open manometer:\[P_X = P_{atm} + \sum(\rho\, g\, h)\text{ of all fluid columns between X and open surface}\]\[\rho = \text{SG} \times 1000\text{ kg/m}^3\]

3. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Convert heights: \(h_{oil} = 0.75\text{ m}\), \(h_{Hg} = 0.25\text{ m}\).
  2. Oil pressure contribution:\[P_{oil} = 0.8 \times 1000 \times 9.81 \times 0.75 = 5886\text{ Pa} = 5.886\text{ kN/m}^2\]
  3. Mercury pressure contribution:\[P_{Hg} = 13.6 \times 1000 \times 9.81 \times 0.25 = 33354\text{ Pa} = 33.354\text{ kN/m}^2\]
  4. Gauge pressure:\[P_{gauge} = 5.886 + 33.354 = 39.24\text{ kN/m}^2\]
  5. Absolute pressure:\[P_X = 101.3 + 39.24 = 140.54 \approx 140.5\text{ kN/m}^2\]

Common Pitfall: Wrong sign convention or forgetting to convert cm to m.

4. Final Answer:

\(P_X = \mathbf{140.5}\text{ kN/m}^2\) | Accepted range: 140.0 to 141.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A compound symmetrical open channel section as shown in the figure has a maximum of _________ critical depth(s).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow — Compound Channels

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: A standard symmetrical compound open channel section.
  • Aim: Identify the maximum possible number of critical depths such a channel can experience.

2. Core Concepts:

  • Specific Energy: \(E = y + \dfrac{\alpha Q^2}{2g A^2}\)
  • Froude Number: \(F^2 = \dfrac{\alpha Q^2 T}{g A^3}\). Critical flow occurs when \(F = 1\).
  • Hydraulic behaviour in compound channels: When water level just spills over the main channel banks into the flood plains, there is a sudden and massive jump in the top width (\(T\)), while the flow area (\(A\)) continues to increase gradually.

3. Solution Method:

Analyze the physical behavior of the specific energy curve and Froude number variations as depth \(y\) increases from the main channel into the flood plains.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Flow contained in main channel (\(y < y_m\)): The channel behaves like a simple rectangular section. It yields one potential critical depth where \(E\) is minimal.
  2. Water overtopping the bank (\(y \ge y_m\)): The top width \(T\) abruptly increases from \(B_m\) to \((B_m + 2B_f)\). Since \(T\) is in the numerator of the Froude number equation, \(F\) spikes sharply. A flow that was subcritical (\(F < 1\)) inside the main channel can suddenly become supercritical (\(F > 1\)) just over the flood plain.
  3. Flow rising further in the floodplain: As depth increases further, the wetted area \(A\) grows. The \(A^3\) term in the denominator overtakes the constant wide \(T\), driving \(F\) back below 1. This crossing provides another critical flow state.
  4. Conclusion: Because the \(E\)-\(y\) curve takes a localized zig-zag (or "S") shape due to the flood plains, it can possess up to three local extremes — giving a maximum of 3 critical depths.

5. Final Answer:

Maximum number of critical depths = 3 | Option(s): A

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q44
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The critical flow condition in a channel is given by _________.
[Note: \( \alpha \) – kinetic energy correction factor; \( Q \) – discharge; \( A_c \) – cross-sectional area of flow at critical flow condition; \( T_c \) – top width of flow at critical flow condition; \( g \) – acceleration due to gravity]
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow — Critical Flow

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Application
  • Given Data: Variables \(\alpha,\ Q,\ A_c,\ T_c,\ g\).
  • Aim: Derive or identify the exact analytical condition for critical flow in an open channel.

2. Core Concepts:

  • Specific Energy equation: \(E = y + \dfrac{\alpha Q^2}{2g A^2}\)
  • Calculus of Critical Flow: Critical depth occurs at the state of minimum specific energy for a constant discharge \(Q\). Therefore, \(\dfrac{dE}{dy} = 0\).

3. Solution Method:

Differentiate the specific energy equation with respect to depth \(y\) and set the equation to zero to solve for the critical state relation.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Differentiate Specific Energy:\[\dfrac{dE}{dy} = \dfrac{d}{dy}\left[y + \dfrac{\alpha Q^2}{2g}\left(A^{-2}\right)\right]\]
  2. Apply the chain rule:\[\dfrac{dE}{dy} = 1 + \left(\dfrac{\alpha Q^2}{2g}\right)\left(-2A^{-3}\right)\dfrac{dA}{dy}\]
  3. Relate Area and Depth: The infinitesimal change in area with respect to depth is the top width \(T\).\[\dfrac{dA}{dy} = T_c\]
  4. Equate to Zero: Set the derivative to zero and substitute \(T_c\):\[1 - \dfrac{\alpha Q^2 \cdot T_c}{g A_c^3} = 0\]
  5. Rearrange:\[\dfrac{\alpha Q^2}{g} = \dfrac{A_c^3}{T_c}\]

5. Final Answer:

\(\dfrac{\alpha Q^2}{g} = \dfrac{A_c^3}{T_c}\) | Option(s): A

For a curved surface immersed in a stationary liquid, the vertical component of the force on the curved surface is equal to the weight of the liquid above it

structuredOptions.text: The thickness of a turbulent boundary layer on a flat plate kept parallel to the flow direction is proportional to the square root of the distance from the leading edge
structuredOptions.html: The thickness of a turbulent boundary layer on a flat plate kept parallel to the flow direction is proportional to the square root of the distance from the leading edge

structuredOptions.text: If the streamlines and equipotential lines of a source are interchanged with each other, the resulting flow will be a sink
structuredOptions.html: If the streamlines and equipotential lines of a source are interchanged with each other, the resulting flow will be a sink

structuredOptions.label: D

structuredOptions.html: For flow through circular pipes, the momentum correction factor for laminar flow is larger than that for turbulent flow

questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Boundary Layer & Fluid Flow

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension & Analysis
  • Given Data: Four theoretical statements regarding boundary layer theory, kinematics, fluid statics, and pipe flow.
  • Aim: Identify the TRUE statement(s) among the given options (Multiple Select Question).

2. Core Concepts & Solution Method:

Statement (A): Thickness of turbulent boundary layer (\(\delta\))
For a flat plate parallel to the flow, the boundary layer thickness grows as:

  • Laminar flow: \(\delta \propto x^{1/2}\) (Blasius solution)
  • Turbulent flow: \(\delta \propto x^{4/5}\) (i.e., \(x^{0.8}\)), derived from the 1/7th power velocity law.

The statement claims turbulent thickness is proportional to \(x^{1/2}\). This is incorrect. (FALSE)

Statement (B): Interchange of streamlines and equipotential lines of a source
For a 2D source, streamlines are radial straight lines and equipotential lines are concentric circles. If interchanged, streamlines become concentric circles — representing a Free Vortex, not a sink. (FALSE)

Statement (C): Vertical force on a curved surface
The vertical component of hydrostatic force equals the weight of the fluid volume physically or virtually enclosed above the curved surface up to the free surface. This is a direct statement of fundamental fluid statics. (TRUE)

Statement (D): Momentum correction factor (\(\beta\))
\[\beta = \dfrac{1}{A V_{avg}^2}\int u^2\, dA\]

  • Laminar flow (parabolic profile): \(\beta = \dfrac{4}{3} \approx 1.33\)
  • Turbulent flow (flat profile): \(\beta \approx 1.01\) to \(1.05\)
Since \(1.33 > 1.05\), \(\beta\) for laminar flow is indeed larger than for turbulent flow. (TRUE)

3. Final Answer:

Statements (C) and (D) are true | Option(s): C, D

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q62
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A catchment may be idealized as a circle of radius 30 km. There are five rain gauges, one at the center of the catchment and four on the boundary (equi-spaced), as shown in the figure (not to scale).
The annual rainfall recorded at these gauges in a particular year are given below.
GaugeG₁G₂G₃G₄G₅
Rainfall (mm)910930925895905

Using the Thiessen polygon method, what is the average rainfall (in mm, rounded off to two decimal places) over the catchment in that year? _________________
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Precipitation & Mean Areal Rainfall

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Catchment shape: Circle with radius \(R = 30\text{ km}\)
    • 5 Rain gauges: \(G_1\) at the center; \(G_2, G_3, G_4, G_5\) on the boundary, equi-spaced (\(90^\circ\) apart).
    • Rainfall records: \(P_1 = 910\text{ mm}\), \(P_2 = 930\text{ mm}\), \(P_3 = 925\text{ mm}\), \(P_4 = 895\text{ mm}\), \(P_5 = 905\text{ mm}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the average rainfall over the catchment using the Thiessen polygon method.

2. Core Concepts:

  • Thiessen Polygon Method: Assigns an area (weight) to each gauge. Polygons are constructed by drawing perpendicular bisectors to lines connecting adjacent gauges.
  • Average Rainfall (\(\bar{P}\)):\[\bar{P} = \dfrac{\sum(A_i P_i)}{\sum A_i} = \sum(W_i P_i)\]where \(W_i = \dfrac{A_i}{A_{total}}\).

3. Solution Method:

  1. Establish the geometry to find the area represented by the central gauge (\(G_1\)).
  2. Determine the area represented by the four outer gauges (\(G_2\) to \(G_5\)) using symmetry.
  3. Calculate the respective weights (\(W_i\)) for each gauge.
  4. Compute the weighted average rainfall.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Total Catchment Area:\[A_{total} = \pi R^2\]
  2. Polygon Area for Central Gauge (\(G_1\)):
    With \(G_1\) at origin and outer gauges at \((0,R),\ (R,0),\ (0,-R),\ (-R,0)\), the perpendicular bisectors of lines from \(G_1\) to each outer gauge form the lines \(y = \pm R/2\) and \(x = \pm R/2\) — a square of side \(R\).\[A_1 = R \times R = R^2\](The square lies entirely within the circular catchment since the maximum distance from center to corner is \(R/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707R < R\).)
  3. Polygon Areas for Outer Gauges (\(G_2\) to \(G_5\)):\[\text{Remaining Area} = \pi R^2 - R^2 = R^2(\pi - 1)\]\[A_{outer} = \dfrac{R^2(\pi-1)}{4} \quad \text{(by symmetry)}\]
  4. Calculate Thiessen Weights:\[W_1 = \dfrac{R^2}{\pi R^2} = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \approx 0.31831\]\[W_{outer} = \dfrac{(\pi-1)/4}{\pi} = \dfrac{\pi-1}{4\pi} \approx 0.17042\]Check: \(\dfrac{1}{\pi} + 4 \times \dfrac{\pi-1}{4\pi} = \dfrac{1 + \pi - 1}{\pi} = 1.0\) ✓
  5. Compute Average Rainfall (\(\bar{P}\)):\[\bar{P} = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\times 910 + \dfrac{\pi-1}{4\pi}\times(930 + 925 + 895 + 905)\]\[\bar{P} = \dfrac{910}{\pi} + \dfrac{(\pi-1)\times 3655}{4\pi}\]\[\bar{P} = \dfrac{3640 + 3655\pi - 3655}{4\pi} = \dfrac{3655\pi - 15}{4\pi}\]\[\bar{P} = \dfrac{3655}{4} - \dfrac{15}{4\pi} = 913.75 - 1.1937 = 912.556...\text{ mm}\]

5. Final Answer:

\(\bar{P} = \mathbf{912.56}\text{ mm}\) | Accepted key range: 912.28 to 912.82

Hydrology | Streamflow Measurement

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:

    • Width of each segment: \(W = 1.5\text{ m}\)
    • Depth (\(D\)) and point velocities at \(0.2D\), \(0.6D\), and \(0.8D\) provided for each segment.
  • Aim: Calculate the total discharge (\(Q\)) using the velocity-area method in \(\text{m}^3/\text{s}\).

2. Core Concepts:

  • Velocity-Area Method:\[Q = \sum_{i=1}^{n} q_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(W_i \cdot D_i \cdot V_{avg,i})\]
  • Average Velocity in a Vertical (\(V_{avg}\)):
    • One-point method (velocity at \(0.6D\) only):\[V_{avg} = V_{0.6D}\]
    • Two-point method (velocities at \(0.2D\) and \(0.8D\)):\[V_{avg} = \dfrac{V_{0.2D} + V_{0.8D}}{2}\]

3. Solution Method:

  1. For each segment, determine \(V_{avg}\) using the appropriate rule based on available data points.
  2. Calculate the partial discharge \(q_i = W \times D_i \times V_{avg,i}\) for each segment.
  3. Sum all partial discharges to obtain total discharge \(Q\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q21

questions.question: A rectangular channel with Gradually Varied Flow (GVF) has a changing bed slope. If the change is from a steeper slope to a steep slope, the resulting GVF profile is
options: either S<sub>1</sub> or S<sub>2</sub>, depending on the magnitude of the slopes

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: either S<sub>1</sub> or S<sub>2</sub>, depending on the magnitude of the slopes
structuredOptions.html: either S<sub>1</sub> or S<sub>2</sub>, depending on the magnitude of the slopes

questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics / Open Channel Flow | Gradually Varied Flow Profiles

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Rectangular channel, Gradually Varied Flow (GVF). Bed slope changes from a steeper steep slope to a less steep steep slope.
  • Aim: Identify the resulting GVF profile.

Core Concepts:

  • Steep Slope (S): Bed slope \(S_0 >\) Critical slope \(S_c\). Normal depth \(y_n < y_c\).
  • The term "steeper slope" implies \(S_{01} > S_{02}\), both being steep.
  • From Manning's equation, a steeper slope produces a smaller normal depth: \(y_{n1} < y_{n2}\).
  • Therefore: \(y_{n1} < y_{n2} < y_c\).

GVF Profiles on Steep Slope:

ZoneDepth ConditionProfile
Zone 1\(y > y_c\)S1 (backwater curve)
Zone 2\(y_n < y < y_c\)S2 (drawdown curve)
Zone 3\(y < y_n\)S3 (backwater curve)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Slope Comparison:
    • \(S_{01}\) (Steeper) \(> S_{02}\) (Steep), implying \(y_{n1} < y_{n2}\).
    • Both normal depths are below critical depth: \(y_{n1} < y_{n2} < y_c\).
  2. Flow Profile on Slope 2:
    • Flow arrives at the break in slope with depth \(\approx y_{n1}\).
    • The equilibrium (normal) depth on Slope 2 is \(y_{n2}\).
    • Since \(y_{n1} < y_{n2}\), the actual depth must increase towards \(y_{n2}\).
    • Check the zone: actual depth \(y \approx y_{n1}\) is less than normal depth \(y_{n2}\) of Slope 2.
    • Condition: \(y < y_n < y_c\) → This corresponds to Zone 3 on a Steep slope.
    • The resulting profile is an S3 curve.

Final Answer:

Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
During a particular stage of the growth of a crop, the consumptive use of water is 2.8 mm/day. The amount of water available in the soil is 50 % of the maximum depth of available water in the root zone. Consider the maximum root zone depth of the crop as 80 mm and the irrigation efficiency as 70 %.

The interval between irrigation (in days) will be ___________. (round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanation:
Irrigation Engineering | Water Requirement & Irrigation Scheduling

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    ParameterValueUnit
    Consumptive use (CU), \(ET_c\)2.8mm/day
    Maximum root zone depth, \(d_{max}\)80mm
    Current available water50% of maximum—
    Irrigation efficiency, \(\eta\)70%
  • Aim: Find irrigation interval in days (nearest integer).

Core Concepts:

IS 5984: 1970 — Code of practice for irrigation scheduling.

Key Definitions:

  • Total Available Water (TAW): Water held between field capacity and permanent wilting point.
  • Readily Available Water (RAW): 50% of TAW (given in this problem).
  • Net Irrigation Requirement (NIR): Water needed to bring soil to field capacity.
  • Gross Irrigation Requirement (GIR): NIR / Efficiency.
  • Irrigation Interval: Time to deplete current available water at the consumptive use rate.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate current available water depth:\[\text{Current Available Water} = 50\% \times 80 \text{ mm} = 0.5 \times 80 = 40 \text{ mm}\]
  2. Calculate irrigation interval:\[\text{Interval} = \dfrac{\text{Current Available Water}}{\text{Consumptive Use per day}} = \dfrac{40 \text{ mm}}{2.8 \text{ mm/day}} = 14.286 \text{ days}\]
  3. Round to nearest integer:\[\text{Interval} \approx 14 \text{ days}\]

Note on Irrigation Efficiency: The efficiency (70%) is used to calculate the gross water to be applied (\(= 40/0.7 = 57.14\) mm), not the interval. The interval depends on when water is depleted (net requirement) at the given consumptive use rate.

Sanity Check: 14–15 days is reasonable; common irrigation intervals are 7–14 days for most field crops. ✓

Note: The answer key shows "MTA" (Marks To All), indicating potential ambiguity — both 14 or 15 days may be acceptable depending on the rounding method used.

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{14 \text{ days}}\] (or 15 depending on rounding) | Accepted: MTA (Marks To All)

questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Irrigation Engineering (Cross-Drainage Works)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: Conceptual statements about the relative configurations of a natural drain (stream) and an irrigation canal.
  • Aim: Identify the correct statement(s) matching standard definitions of cross-drainage works.

Core Concepts:

StructureDescription
AqueductCanal is carried over the natural drain. Drain flows under open channel (atmospheric) conditions.
Syphon AqueductCanal is carried over the drain, but drain flows under syphonic (pipe) pressure because flood level is above canal bed.
Super-passageNatural drain is carried over the irrigation canal. Canal flows under open channel conditions.
Canal SyphonNatural drain is carried over the canal, and the canal flows under syphonic (pressure) action.
Level CrossingCanal and natural drain intersect at the same elevation. Waters intermingle; flow is regulated by cross and head regulators.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  • Option (A): "In an aqueduct, natural drain water goes under the irrigation canal, whereas in a super-passage, natural drain water goes over the irrigation canal." → Matches definitions exactly. ✓ True
  • Option (B): "In a level crossing, natural drain water goes through the irrigation canal." → Since they intersect at the same bed level, water intermingling passes through the crossing section. ✓ True
  • Option (C): "In an aqueduct, natural drain water goes over the irrigation canal." → This is the definition of a super-passage, not an aqueduct. ✗ False
  • Option (D): "In a canal syphon, natural drain water goes through the irrigation canal." → In a canal syphon, the canal is routed under the drain via an inverted syphon; waters do not mix. ✗ False

Final Answer:

Correct Options: (A), (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q57
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Two reservoirs are connected by two parallel pipes of equal length and of diameters 20 cm and 10 cm, as shown in the figure (not drawn to scale). When the difference in the water levels of the reservoirs is 5 m, the ratio of discharge in the larger diameter pipe to the discharge in the smaller diameter pipe is _________. (round off to two decimal places)

(Consider only loss due to friction and neglect all other losses. Assume the friction factor to be the same for both the pipes)
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Flow Through Pipes

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Parallel pipes; \(L_1 = L_2 = L\); \(f_1 = f_2 = f\); \(H = 5\) m; \(d_1 = 20\) cm; \(d_2 = 10\) cm; minor losses neglected.
  • Aim: Find the discharge ratio \(Q_1 / Q_2\).

Core Concepts:

Darcy-Weisbach Equation (in terms of discharge):

\[h_f = \dfrac{8 f L Q^2}{\pi^2 g d^5}\]

Parallel Pipes Principle: Head losses are equal across both pipes: \(h_{f1} = h_{f2}\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Equate Head Losses:\[\dfrac{8fL Q_1^2}{\pi^2 g d_1^5} = \dfrac{8fL Q_2^2}{\pi^2 g d_2^5}\]
  2. Simplify (cancel \(8, f, L, \pi^2, g\)):
    \[\dfrac{Q_1^2}{d_1^5} = \dfrac{Q_2^2}{d_2^5} \implies \left(\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{d_1}{d_2}\right)^5\]\[\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} = \left(\dfrac{d_1}{d_2}\right)^{5/2}\]
  3. Calculate the ratio:\[\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} = \left(\dfrac{20}{10}\right)^{2.5} = (2)^{2.5} = 2^2 \times \sqrt{2} = 4 \times 1.4142 = 5.657\]

Note: The 5 m head difference is redundant data here, as it cancels out in the ratio.

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} \approx 5.66}\] Accepted range: 5.60 to 5.70

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q58
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Depth of water flowing in a 3 m wide rectangular channel is 2 m. The channel carries a discharge of 12 m³/s. Take \(g = 9.8\) m/s².

The bed width (in m) at contraction, which just causes the critical flow, is ________ without changing the upstream water level. (round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
Open Channel Flow | Specific Energy & Critical Flow

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data: Rectangular channel; upstream width \(B_1 = 3\) m; upstream depth \(y_1 = 2\) m; discharge \(Q = 12\) m³/s; \(g = 9.8\) m/s².
  • Aim: Find the contracted width \(B_2\) that just induces critical flow without altering the upstream pool level (choking threshold).

Core Concepts:

  • Specific Energy: \(E = y + \dfrac{V^2}{2g}\)
  • Choking Limit State: At the minimum contracted width, critical flow occurs exactly at the throat with \(E_2 = E_1\) (no upstream backwater).
  • Critical Flow in Rectangular Channel:\[E_c = \dfrac{3}{2}y_c \implies y_c = \dfrac{2}{3}E_c\]\[B_c = \sqrt{\dfrac{Q^2}{g \cdot y_c^3}}\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Upstream Velocity and Specific Energy:\[V_1 = \dfrac{Q}{B_1 y_1} = \dfrac{12}{3 \times 2} = 2 \text{ m/s}\]\[E_1 = 2 + \dfrac{2^2}{2 \times 9.8} = 2 + \dfrac{4}{19.6} = 2 + 0.2041 = 2.2041 \text{ m}\]
  2. Critical Depth at Contraction Threshold:\[E_c = E_1 = 2.2041 \text{ m}\]\[y_c = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 2.2041 = 1.4694 \text{ m}\]
  3. Solve for Minimum Contracted Width:\[B_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{Q^2}{g \cdot y_c^3}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{144}{9.8 \times (1.4694)^3}}\]\[= \sqrt{\dfrac{144}{9.8 \times 3.1725}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{144}{31.090}} = \sqrt{4.632} = 2.152 \text{ m}\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{B_2 \approx 2.15 \text{ m}}\] Accepted range: 2.05 to 2.35
