structuredOptions.text: \( P_A \) is always greater than \( P_T \)
structuredOptions.html: \( P_A \) is always greater than \( P_T \)

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: \( P_A \) is always equal to \( P_T \)
structuredOptions.html: \( P_A \) is always equal to \( P_T \)

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: There is no definite relationship between \( P_A \) and \( P_T \)
structuredOptions.html: There is no definite relationship between \( P_A \) and \( P_T \)

questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Precipitation

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Catchment shape: Rectangular
    • Rain gauges: 3 gauges at arbitrary locations inside
    • Estimation methods: Arithmetic Mean (\(P_A\)) and Thiessen Polygon (\(P_T\))
  • Aim: Determine the relationship between \(P_A\) and \(P_T\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Arithmetic Mean Method (\(P_A\)): Straight average — each gauge has equal weight (\(1/3\)).\[P_A = \dfrac{P_1 + P_2 + P_3}{3} \]
  • Thiessen Polygon Method (\(P_T\)): Area-weighted average — each gauge's influence depends on its polygon area \(A_i\).\[P_T = \dfrac{A_1 P_1 + A_2 P_2 + A_3 P_3}{A_{total}} \]

4. Solution Method:

Evaluate whether independent variables (rainfall depth \(P_i\) and geographical placement \(A_i\)) force a specific mathematical inequality.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Gauges are at arbitrary locations \(\implies\) unequal polygon areas (\(A_1 \neq A_2 \neq A_3\)).
  2. Arithmetic mean rigidly assigns weight \(1/3\) to each gauge regardless of spatial coverage.
  3. Thiessen method dynamically assigns weights \(A_i/A\).
  4. If a gauge with high rainfall covers a small polygon (\(A_i/A < 1/3\)), \(P_A\) over-weights it \(\implies P_A > P_T\).
  5. Conversely, if a gauge with high rainfall covers a dominant polygon (\(A_i/A > 1/3\)), \(P_T\) over-weights it \(\implies P_A < P_T\).
  6. Since rainfall depths and arbitrary areas are independent random variables, neither method intrinsically overestimates the other in all conditions.

6. Final Answer:

There is no definite relationship between \(P_A\) and \(P_T\) | Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q22
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A circular duct carrying water gradually contracts from a diameter of 30 cm to 15 cm. The figure (not drawn to scale) shows the arrangement of differential manometer attached to the duct.

When the water flows, the differential manometer shows a deflection of 8 cm of mercury (Hg). The values of specific gravity of mercury and water are 13.6 and 1.0, respectively. Consider the acceleration due to gravity, \( g = 9.81\ m/s^2 \). Assuming frictionless flow, the flow rate (in \( m^3/s \), round off to 3 decimal places) through the duct is ________
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Fluid Dynamics (Venturimeter)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Upstream diameter \(D_1 = 30\) cm \(= 0.3\) m; Contracted diameter \(D_2 = 15\) cm \(= 0.15\) m
    • Manometer reading \(x = 8\) cm \(= 0.08\) m; \(S_m = 13.6\), \(S_w = 1.0\)
    • \(g = 9.81\) m/s\(^2\); Frictionless flow \(\implies C_d = 1.0\)
  • Aim: Find volumetric flow rate \(Q\) in m\(^3\)/s (3 decimal places).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Continuity Equation: \(Q = A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2\)
  • Bernoulli's Equation (horizontal): \(h = \dfrac{P_1 - P_2}{\gamma_w} = \dfrac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2g}\)
  • Manometry: \(h = x\left(\dfrac{S_m}{S_w} - 1\right)\)
  • Discharge Formula: \(Q = C_d\dfrac{A_1 A_2 \sqrt{2gh}}{\sqrt{A_1^2 - A_2^2}}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Compute cross-sectional areas \(A_1\) and \(A_2\).
  2. Compute differential pressure head \(h\) from manometer reading.
  3. Input values into the discharge equation.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Areas:\[A_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.3)^2 = 0.070686\text{ m}^2, \quad A_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.15)^2 = 0.017671\text{ m}^2 \]
  2. Differential Head:\[h = 0.08 \times (13.6 - 1) = 0.08 \times 12.6 = 1.008\text{ m of water} \]
  3. Denominator term:\[\sqrt{A_1^2 - A_2^2} = \sqrt{(0.070686)^2 - (0.017671)^2} = 0.068436\text{ m}^2 \]
  4. Velocity factor:\[\sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 1.008} = \sqrt{19.777} = 4.4471\text{ m/s} \]
  5. Flow rate:\[Q = 1.0 \times \dfrac{0.070686 \times 0.017671}{0.068436} \times 4.4471 = 0.018250 \times 4.4471 \approx 0.081\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]

6. Final Answer:

\(Q = 0.081\) m\(^3\)/s | Accepted key range: 0.078 to 0.085

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q23
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The probability that the annual maximum flood discharge will exceed 25000 \( m^3/s \), at least once in next 5 years is found to be 0.25. The return period of this flood event (in years, round off to 1 decimal place) is ________
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Floods / Probability

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Annual maximum flood discharge \(> 25000\) m\(^3\)/s
    • Probability of event occurring at least once (Risk, \(R\)) \(= 0.25\)
    • Time span \((n) = 5\) years
  • Aim: Calculate the return period \(T\) in years (rounded to 1 decimal place).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Return Period (\(T\)): Statistical average time between occurrences of a given event.
  • Annual Exceedance Probability: \(p = 1/T\)
  • Hydrological Risk (\(R\)):\[R = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^n \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Substitute known \(R\) and \(n\) into the risk equation.
  2. Isolate and solve for \(\left(1 - 1/T\right)\).
  3. Take the reciprocal to find \(T\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Substitute knowns:\[0.25 = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^5 \]
  2. Rearrange:\[\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^5 = 0.75 \]
  3. Take the 5th root:\[1 - \dfrac{1}{T} = (0.75)^{0.2} \approx 0.94409 \]
  4. Solve for \(p\):\[\dfrac{1}{T} = 1 - 0.94409 = 0.05591 \]
  5. Return period:\[T = \dfrac{1}{0.05591} \approx 17.9\text{ years} \]

6. Final Answer:

Return Period \(T = 17.9\) years | Accepted key range: 17.8 to 18.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q28
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A rectangular open channel has a width of 5 m and a bed slope of 0.001. For a uniform flow of depth 2 m, the velocity is 2 m/s. The Manning’s roughness coefficient for the channel is
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics & Hydraulics | Open Channel Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Width \((B) = 5\) m
    • Flow depth \((y) = 2\) m
    • Velocity \((V) = 2\) m/s
    • Bed slope \((S_0) = 0.001\)
  • Aim: To determine the Manning's roughness coefficient \((n)\).

3. Core Concepts:

Manning's Equation for Uniform Flow:

\[V = \dfrac{1}{n} R^{2/3} S_0^{1/2} \]

Hydraulic Radius \((R)\): \(R = \dfrac{A}{P}\), where \(A\) is the cross-sectional area and \(P\) is the wetted perimeter.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Compute Cross-sectional Area \((A)\) and Wetted Perimeter \((P)\):
    \[A = B \times y = 5 \text{ m} \times 2 \text{ m} = 10 \text{ m}^2 \]\[P = B + 2y = 5 \text{ m} + 2(2 \text{ m}) = 9 \text{ m} \]
  2. Compute Hydraulic Radius \((R)\):
    \[R = \dfrac{A}{P} = \dfrac{10}{9} \approx 1.1111 \text{ m} \]
  3. Rearrange Manning's formula and solve for \(n\):
    \[n = \dfrac{R^{2/3} S_0^{1/2}}{V} \]\[n = \dfrac{(10/9)^{2/3} \times (0.001)^{1/2}}{2} \]\[n = \dfrac{1.07276 \times 0.03162}{2} = \dfrac{0.03392}{2} = 0.01696 \]
    Rounding off to three decimal places gives \(n \approx 0.017\).

5. Final Answer:

\(n = 0.017\) | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q49
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The hyetograph of a storm event of duration 140 minutes is shown in the figure.

The infiltration capacity at the start of this event (t = 0) is 17 mm/hour, which linearly decreases to 10 mm/hour after 40 minutes duration. As the event progresses, the infiltration rate further drops down linearly to attain a value of 4 mm/hour at t = 100 minutes and remains constant thereafter till the end of the storm event. The value of the infiltration index, φ (in mm/hour, round off to 2 decimal places), is ________
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Infiltration & Runoff

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Storm duration \(= 140\) min
    • Rainfall intensity (\(i\)) in 20-min intervals (mm/h): 4, 8, 15, 10, 8, 3, 1
    • Infiltration capacity (\(f_c\)) curve:
      • \(t = 0\) to \(40\) min: 17 to 10 mm/h
      • \(t = 40\) to \(100\) min: 10 to 4 mm/h
      • \(t > 100\) min: Constant at 4 mm/h
  • Aim: Calculate the \(\phi\)-index (in mm/h).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Actual Infiltration vs. Rainfall: Actual infiltration rate \(f(t) = \min(i(t),\ f_c(t))\).
  • Direct Runoff (\(R\)): Runoff occurs only when \(i(t) > f_c(t)\). Total runoff is the area between the hyetograph and the actual infiltration curve.
  • \(\phi\)-index: The constant, average infiltration rate during periods of rainfall excess such that the calculated runoff strictly equals the actual observed runoff:\[R = \sum (i_j - \phi) \cdot \Delta t \quad \text{for intervals where } i_j > \phi \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Divide the storm into 20-minute (\(\dfrac{1}{3}\) hour) intervals.
  2. Determine the average \(f_c\) for each interval.
  3. Calculate actual runoff generated in each interval and sum to get total Direct Runoff (\(R\)).
  4. Formulate the \(\phi\)-index equation iteratively by guessing a range for \(\phi\) to determine which rainfall blocks actively produce runoff.
  5. Solve for \(\phi\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate Runoff per Interval (\(\Delta t = 20\text{ min} = \dfrac{1}{3}\text{ h}\))

Interval (min)\(i\) (mm/h)Avg \(f_c\) (mm/h)\(i\) vs \(f_c\)Runoff (mm)
0 – 20415.25\(i < f_c\)0
20 – 40811.75\(i < f_c\)0
40 – 60159\(i > f_c\)\((15-9) \times \dfrac{1}{3} = 2\) mm
60 – 80107\(i > f_c\)\((10-7) \times \dfrac{1}{3} = 1\) mm
80 – 10085\(i > f_c\)\((8-5) \times \dfrac{1}{3} = 1\) mm
100 – 12034\(i < f_c\)0
120 – 14014\(i < f_c\)0

Total Runoff (\(R\)) \(= 2 + 1 + 1 = 4\) mm

Step 2: Calculate the \(\phi\)-index

Assume \(\phi\) lies between \(4\) mm/h and \(8\) mm/h. Therefore, only intervals with \(i \ge 8\) mm/h contribute to runoff:
Contributing intervals: 20–40 (\(i=8\)), 40–60 (\(i=15\)), 60–80 (\(i=10\)), 80–100 (\(i=8\)).

  • Effective rainfall duration: \(t_e = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\) hours
  • Total effective rainfall: \(P_e = (8+15+10+8) \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{41}{3}\) mm

Apply the \(\phi\)-index formula:

\[R = P_e - \phi \cdot t_e \]\[4 = \dfrac{41}{3} - \phi \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right) \]

Multiply through by 3:

\[12 = 41 - 4\phi \implies 4\phi = 29 \implies \phi = \dfrac{29}{4} = 7.25\text{ mm/h} \]

Sanity check: \(7.25\) mm/h correctly falls in the assumed \((4, 8]\) range, validating the assumption.

6. Final Answer:

\(\phi\text{-index} = 7.25\) mm/h | Accepted key range: 7.20 to 7.30

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Two water reservoirs are connected by a siphon (running full) of total length 5000 m and diameter of 0.10 m, as shown below (figure not drawn to scale).

The inlet leg length of the siphon to its summit is 2000 m. The difference in the water surface levels of the two reservoirs is 5 m. Assume the permissible minimum absolute pressure at the summit of siphon to be 2.5 m of water when running full. Given: friction factor f = 0.02 throughout, atmospheric pressure = 10.3 m of water, and acceleration due to gravity g = 9.81 m/s². Considering only major loss using Darcy-Weisbach equation, the maximum height of the summit of siphon from the water level of upper reservoir, h (in m, round off to 1 decimal place) is ________
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pipe Flow / Siphon

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Total pipe length \((L) = 5000\) m
    • Pipe diameter \((d) = 0.10\) m
    • Inlet leg length to summit \((L_1) = 2000\) m
    • Head difference between reservoirs \((\Delta H) = 5\) m
    • Min. absolute pressure at summit \((P_{s,abs}/\gamma) = 2.5\) m of water
    • Friction factor \((f) = 0.02\)
    • Atmospheric pressure head \((P_{atm}/\gamma) = 10.3\) m of water
    • \(g = 9.81\) m/s\(^2\)
  • Aim: Find the maximum height of the summit from the upper reservoir water level \((h)\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Darcy-Weisbach Equation for major head loss:\[h_f = \dfrac{f \cdot L \cdot v^2}{2 \cdot g \cdot d} \]
  • Total System Head Loss: For reservoirs connected by a pipe, the total head loss equals the difference in water surface elevations (\(\Delta H = 5\) m).
  • Bernoulli's Energy Equation between the upper reservoir surface and the summit — absolute pressure values must be used.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Use the total head loss to find the steady flow velocity (\(v\)) in the siphon.
  2. Apply Bernoulli's equation between the top reservoir surface and the siphon summit, tracking head loss incurred strictly within the inlet leg (\(L_1\)).
  3. Solve the resulting equation for the elevation of the summit (\(h\)).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate the flow velocity (\(v\))

\[\Delta H = \dfrac{f \cdot L \cdot v^2}{2 \cdot g \cdot d} \]\[5 = \dfrac{0.02 \times 5000 \times v^2}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.10} = \dfrac{100\, v^2}{1.962} \]\[v^2 = \dfrac{5 \times 1.962}{100} = 0.0981\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2 \implies v = 0.3132\text{ m/s} \]

Step 2: Calculate head loss in the inlet leg (\(h_{f1}\))

\[h_{f1} = \dfrac{f \cdot L_1 \cdot v^2}{2 \cdot g \cdot d} = \dfrac{0.02 \times 2000 \times 0.0981}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.10} = \dfrac{3.924}{1.962} = 2.0\text{ m} \]

Step 3: Apply Bernoulli's Equation
Point 1 = upper reservoir surface (datum, \(z_1 = 0\), \(v_1 \approx 0\)); Point S = siphon summit (\(z_S = h\), \(v_S = v\)).

\[\dfrac{P_1}{\gamma} + \dfrac{v_1^2}{2g} + z_1 = \dfrac{P_S}{\gamma} + \dfrac{v_S^2}{2g} + z_S + h_{f1} \]\[10.3 + 0 + 0 = 2.5 + \dfrac{0.0981}{2 \times 9.81} + h + 2.0 \]\[10.3 = 2.5 + 0.005 + h + 2.0 = 4.505 + h \]\[h = 10.3 - 4.505 = 5.795\text{ m} \approx 5.8\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Maximum summit height \(h = 5.8\) m | Accepted key range: 5.7 to 5.9

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: Consider a laminar flow in the x-direction between two infinite parallel plates (Couette flow). The lower plate is stationary and the upper plate is moving with a velocity of 1 cm/s in the x-direction. The distance between the plates is 5 mm and the dynamic viscosity of the fluid is 0.01 N·s/m². If the shear stress on the lower plate is zero, the pressure gradient, \( \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} \), (in N/m² per m, round off to 1 decimal place) is ________
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Viscous Flow (Couette Flow)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Velocity of upper plate \((U) = 1\) cm/s \(= 0.01\) m/s
    • Distance between plates \((h) = 5\) mm \(= 0.005\) m
    • Dynamic viscosity \((\mu) = 0.01\) N⋅s/m\(^2\)
    • Shear stress on lower plate \((\tau_{y=0}) = 0\)
  • Aim: Calculate the pressure gradient \(\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}\) in N/m\(^2\) per m.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Navier-Stokes Equation for 1D Laminar Flow: For fully developed steady flow between parallel plates, pressure forces balance viscous shear forces:\[\mu \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} \]
  • Newton's Law of Viscosity: \(\tau = \mu\, \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Integrate the governing differential equation twice to get the general velocity profile \(u(y)\).
  2. Apply boundary conditions: \(u(0)=0\) (stationary bottom plate) and \(u(h)=U\) (moving top plate) to find integration constants.
  3. Differentiate \(u(y)\) to find the shear stress expression \(\tau(y)\).
  4. Set \(\tau\) at \(y=0\) equal to 0 and solve for \(\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Integrating \(\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = \dfrac{1}{\mu}\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}\) twice:

\[u(y) = \dfrac{1}{2\mu} \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} y^2 + C_1 y + C_2 \]

Apply Boundary Conditions:

  1. At \(y=0,\ u=0 \implies C_2 = 0\)
  2. At \(y=h,\ u=U \implies C_1 = \dfrac{U}{h} - \dfrac{1}{2\mu}\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}h\)

Shear stress profile:

\[\tau(y) = \mu\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}y + \mu C_1 \]

Given \(\tau(0) = 0\):

\[\mu C_1 = 0 \implies C_1 = 0 \]

Substituting \(C_1 = 0\) into the second boundary condition:

\[0 = \dfrac{U}{h} - \dfrac{1}{2\mu}\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}h \implies \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} = \dfrac{2\mu U}{h^2} \]

Substituting values:

\[\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.01 \times 0.01}{(0.005)^2} = \dfrac{0.0002}{0.000025} = 8.0\text{ N/m}^3 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} = 8.0\) N/m\(^3\) | Accepted key range: 7.9 to 8.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q12
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A solid sphere of radius, \(r\), and made of material with density, \(\rho_s\), is moving through the atmosphere (constant pressure, \(p\)) with a velocity, \(v\). The net force ONLY due to atmospheric pressure (\(F_p\)) acting on the sphere at any time, \(t\), is
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Fluid Statics / Hydrostatics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Solid sphere of radius \(= r\)
    • Material density \(= \rho_s\)
    • Atmospheric pressure \(= p\) (Constant)
    • Velocity \(= v\)
  • Aim: Determine the net force due only to atmospheric pressure (\(F_p\)) acting on the sphere at any time \(t\).

3. Core Concepts:

Pressure Force on a Closed Surface: The net pressure force exerted by a fluid on a fully submerged closed surface is the integral of the pressure over the surface area:

\[\mathbf{F_p} = \iint_{A} -p \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot dA \]

Divergence Theorem / Archimedes' Principle: A constant pressure field has a pressure gradient \(\nabla p = 0\). Using the Divergence theorem:

\[\iint_{A} -p \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot dA = \iiint_{V} -\nabla p \cdot dV \]

4. Solution Method:

Since the atmospheric pressure \(p\) is uniform (constant) all around the sphere, the inward forces exerted on any infinitesimally small area of the sphere are exactly counterbalanced by the inward pressure forces on the diametrically opposite area. Therefore, the net resultant force generated by a uniform pressure field over a closed 3D body is always zero.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Set up the integral for net force: \(F_p = \oint -p \cdot d\mathbf{A}\).
  2. Since \(p\) is constant, take it out of the integral: \(F_p = -p \oint d\mathbf{A}\).
  3. The integral of the outward normal vector over any closed geometrical surface is strictly zero: \(\oint d\mathbf{A} = 0\).
  4. Result: \(F_p = -p(0) = 0\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: zero | Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q13
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The velocity field in a flow system is given by \(v = 2\mathbf{i} + (x+y)\mathbf{j} + (xyz)\mathbf{k}\). The acceleration of the fluid at \((1, 1, 2)\) is
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Fluid Kinematics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Velocity field \(\mathbf{v} = 2\,\mathbf{i} + (x+y)\,\mathbf{j} + (xyz)\,\mathbf{k}\)
    • Coordinates for evaluation: \((x, y, z) = (1, 1, 2)\)
  • Aim: Calculate the total acceleration vector of the fluid at the given coordinates.

3. Core Concepts:

Total Acceleration: \(\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{a_{local}} + \mathbf{a_{convective}}\)

Since the velocity field has no time \(t\) variable, flow is steady. Hence, local acceleration \(\dfrac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} = 0\).

Convective Acceleration Components:

\[a_x = u\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + v\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} + w\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} \]\[a_y = u\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} + v\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y} + w\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial z} \]\[a_z = u\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} + v\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} + w\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial z} \]

4. Solution Method:

Extract velocity components \(u, v, w\). Calculate their partial derivatives with respect to \(x, y, z\). Substitute these and the specific coordinate values \((1, 1, 2)\) into the convective acceleration formulas to find \(a_x\), \(a_y\), and \(a_z\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Extract Components:
    \(u = 2\), \(v = x + y\), \(w = xyz\)
  2. Evaluate Partial Derivatives:
    \(\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0,\quad \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 0,\quad \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} = 0\)
    \(\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} = 1,\quad \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y} = 1,\quad \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial z} = 0\)
    \(\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} = yz,\quad \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} = xz,\quad \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial z} = xy\)
  3. Calculate \(a_x,\, a_y,\, a_z\) parametrically:
    \(a_x = (2)(0) + (x+y)(0) + (xyz)(0) = 0\)
    \(a_y = (2)(1) + (x+y)(1) + (xyz)(0) = 2 + x + y\)
    \(a_z = (2)(yz) + (x+y)(xz) + (xyz)(xy)\)
  4. Substitute Coordinates \((1, 1, 2)\):
    \(a_x = 0\)
    \(a_y = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4\)
    \(a_z = 2(1 \times 2) + (1+1)(1 \times 2) + (1 \times 1 \times 2)(1 \times 1)\)\[a_z = 2(2) + 2(2) + 2(1) = 4 + 4 + 2 = 10 \]
  5. Form the Resulting Vector:\[\mathbf{a} = 0\,\mathbf{i} + 4\,\mathbf{j} + 10\,\mathbf{k} = 4\,\mathbf{j} + 10\,\mathbf{k} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(4\,\mathbf{j} + 10\,\mathbf{k}\) | Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q14
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: An inflow hydrograph is routed through a reservoir to produce an outflow hydrograph. The peak flow of the inflow hydrograph is \(P_I\) and the time of occurrence of the peak is \(t_I\). The peak flow of the outflow hydrograph is \(P_O\) and the time of occurrence of the peak is \(t_O\). Which one of the following statements is correct?
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Flood Routing

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Inflow peak flow \(= P_I\), Time of inflow peak \(= t_I\)
    • Outflow peak flow \(= P_O\), Time of outflow peak \(= t_O\)
  • Aim: Determine the relationship between \(P_I\) and \(P_O\), and \(t_I\) and \(t_O\) during reservoir routing.

3. Core Concepts:

Reservoir Routing Principles: As a flood wave passes through a reservoir, the temporary storage of water dynamically alters the hydrograph.

Attenuation: The reduction in the peak discharge. The peak of the outflow hydrograph is generally lower than the peak of the inflow hydrograph due to volume absorbed by reservoir storage.

Translation/Lag: The delay in the time of the peak discharge. The outflow peak occurs later than the inflow peak.

4. Solution Method:

By the continuity equation for a reservoir with a passive spillway \(\left(I - Q = \dfrac{dS}{dt}\right)\), the outflow reaches its peak when the outflow rate exactly equals the inflow rate \(\left(I = Q,\text{ making } \dfrac{dS}{dt} = 0\right)\). This intersection mathematically must occur on the falling limb of the inflow hydrograph.
Therefore, the peak of outflow (\(P_O\)) must be physically lower than the peak of inflow (\(P_I\)). Furthermore, because this intersection occurs on the falling limb, the time of the outflow peak (\(t_O\)) occurs strictly after the time of the inflow peak (\(t_I\)).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Evaluate Peak Flow (Attenuation): \(P_O < P_I \implies P_I > P_O\)
  2. Evaluate Peak Time (Lag): \(t_O > t_I \implies t_I < t_O\)
  3. Check options combining both truths: \(P_I > P_O\) and \(t_I < t_O\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(P_I > P_O\) and \(t_I < t_O\) | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q24
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The command area of a canal grows only one crop, i.e., wheat. The base period of wheat is 120 days and its total water requirement, Δ, is 40 cm. If the canal discharge is 2 m³/s, the area, in hectares, rounded off to the nearest integer, which could be irrigated (neglecting all losses) is ______
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Irrigation Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Base period, \(B = 120\) days
    • Total water requirement (Delta), \(\Delta = 40\) cm \(= 0.40\) m
    • Canal discharge, \(Q = 2\) m³/s
  • Aim: Calculate the command area (in hectares) that can be irrigated.

3. Core Concepts:

Volumetric Balance Approach (Foolproof Method):

\[V_{\text{supplied}} = Q \times t \]\[V_{\text{required}} = \text{Area} \times \Delta \]

Duty-Delta Relation (Alternative Method):

\[D = \dfrac{8.64\, B}{\Delta} \quad (D \text{ in ha/cumec},\ B \text{ in days},\ \Delta \text{ in meters}) \]\[\text{Area} = Q \times D \]

4. Solution Method:

Using the volumetric equivalence method avoids forgetting the 8.64 constant. All units are converted strictly to standard SI (meters, seconds) to find the Area in m², then converted to hectares.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Time Conversion:\[B \text{ (in seconds)} = 120 \times 24 \times 3600 = 10{,}368{,}000 \text{ s} \]
  2. Volume Supplied (\(V\)):\[V = Q \times t = 2 \text{ m}^3/\text{s} \times 10{,}368{,}000 \text{ s} = 20{,}736{,}000 \text{ m}^3 \]
  3. Calculate Area in m²:\[V = \text{Area} \times \Delta \implies \text{Area} = \dfrac{20{,}736{,}000}{0.40} = 51{,}840{,}000 \text{ m}^2 \]
  4. Convert to Hectares (\(1 \text{ ha} = 10^4 \text{ m}^2\)):\[\text{Area (ha)} = \dfrac{51{,}840{,}000}{10{,}000} = 5184 \text{ ha} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 5184 | Accepted key range: 5180 to 5190

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q47
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A confined aquifer of 15 m constant thickness is sandwiched between two aquicludes as shown in the figure (not drawn to scale).


The heads indicated by two piezometers P and Q are 55.2 m and 34.1 m, respectively. The aquifer has a hydraulic conductivity of 80 m/day and its effective porosity is 0.25. If the distance between the piezometers is 2500 m, the time taken by the water to travel through the aquifer from piezometer location P to Q (in days, round off to 1 decimal place) is ______
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Groundwater Hydrology

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Aquifer thickness (\(b\)): 15 m (Distractor)
    • Piezometric head at P (\(h_P\)): 55.2 m
    • Piezometric head at Q (\(h_Q\)): 34.1 m
    • Distance between P and Q (\(L\)): 2500 m
    • Hydraulic conductivity (\(K\)): 80 m/day
    • Effective porosity (\(n_e\)): 0.25
  • Aim: Calculate the actual travel time of water from P to Q in days, rounded to 1 decimal place.

3. Core Concepts:

Darcy's Law: Gives the apparent (discharge) velocity \(v\) of water through a porous medium.

\[v = K \cdot i \quad \left(i = \dfrac{\Delta h}{L}\right) \]

Seepage Velocity (True Velocity): Water only travels through the void spaces, so the actual travel speed \(v_s\) is faster than Darcy's velocity.

\[v_s = \dfrac{v}{n_e} \]

Travel Time (\(t\)):

\[t = \dfrac{L}{v_s} \]

Note: The aquifer thickness (15 m) dictates total discharge but is completely irrelevant for evaluating particle travel time.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the head difference (\(\Delta h\)) between the two piezometers.
  2. Compute the hydraulic gradient (\(i\)).
  3. Calculate the Darcy velocity (\(v\)).
  4. Calculate the Seepage velocity (\(v_s\)) using the effective porosity.
  5. Find the travel time by dividing the total length by the seepage velocity.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Calculate Hydraulic Gradient (\(i\))\[\Delta h = h_P - h_Q = 55.2 - 34.1 = 21.1\text{ m} \]\[i = \dfrac{\Delta h}{L} = \dfrac{21.1}{2500} = 0.00844 \]
  2. Step 2: Calculate Darcy Velocity (\(v\))\[v = K \cdot i = 80 \times 0.00844 = 0.6752\text{ m/day} \]
  3. Step 3: Calculate Seepage Velocity (\(v_s\))\[v_s = \dfrac{v}{n_e} = \dfrac{0.6752}{0.25} = 2.7008\text{ m/day} \]
  4. Step 4: Calculate Travel Time (\(t\))\[t = \dfrac{L}{v_s} = \dfrac{2500}{2.7008} = 925.651\text{ days} \approx 925.7\text{ days} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 925.7 days | Accepted key range: 924.0 to 926.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
At the foot of a spillway, water flows at a depth of 23 cm with a velocity of 8.1 m/s, as shown in the figure.


The flow enters as an M-3 profile in the long wide rectangular channel with bed slope = \(\dfrac{1}{1800}\) and Manning’s n = 0.015. A hydraulic jump is formed at a certain distance from the foot of the spillway. Assume the acceleration due to gravity, g = 9.81 m/s². Just before the hydraulic jump, the depth of flow y₁ (in m, round off to 2 decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow (Hydraulic Jump)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Initial depth of flow, \(y_0 = 23\) cm \(= 0.23\) m
    • Initial velocity, \(V_0 = 8.1\) m/s
    • Bed slope, \(S_0 = 1/1800\)
    • Manning's roughness coefficient, \(n = 0.015\)
    • \(g = 9.81\) m/s²
    • Channel type: Long, wide rectangular channel
    • Profile type: M-3 profile (mild slope, supercritical flow)
  • Aim: Find the depth of flow just before the hydraulic jump, \(y_1\).

3. Core Concepts:

Specific Discharge (\(q\)): For a wide rectangular channel, \(q = V_0 y_0\).

Normal Depth (\(y_n\)): The depth the flow will eventually try to reach. Calculated using Manning's equation for a wide channel (\(R \approx y\)):

\[q = \dfrac{1}{n} y_n^{5/3} S_0^{1/2} \]

Hydraulic Jump Conjugate Depths:

\[\dfrac{2q^2}{g} = y_1 y_2 (y_1 + y_2) \]

Jump Location Condition: In an M-3 profile on a long mild slope, the depth after the jump must equal the normal depth: \(y_2 = y_n\).

4. Solution Method & Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Calculate specific discharge (\(q\))\[q = V_0 \times y_0 = 8.1 \times 0.23 = 1.863\text{ m}^2\text{/s/m} \]
  2. Step 2: Determine normal depth (\(y_n\))\[1.863 = \dfrac{1}{0.015} y_n^{5/3} \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{1800}} = 66.667 \times \dfrac{1}{42.426} \cdot y_n^{5/3} = 1.5714\, y_n^{5/3} \]\[y_n^{5/3} = \dfrac{1.863}{1.5714} = 1.1856 \implies y_n = (1.1856)^{3/5} = 1.107\text{ m} \]
  3. Step 3: Solve for depth before the jump (\(y_1\))
    With \(y_2 = y_n = 1.107\) m, using the conjugate depths relation:\[\dfrac{2 \times (1.863)^2}{9.81} = y_1 (1.107)(y_1 + 1.107) \]\[0.7076 = 1.107 y_1^2 + 1.225 y_1 \]Rearranging:\[1.107 y_1^2 + 1.225 y_1 - 0.7076 = 0 \]Solving using the quadratic formula:\[y_1 = \dfrac{-1.225 + \sqrt{(1.225)^2 + 4(1.107)(0.7076)}}{2 \times 1.107} = \dfrac{-1.225 + \sqrt{4.6338}}{2.214} = \dfrac{0.9276}{2.214} = 0.419\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.42 m | Accepted key range: 0.41 to 0.43

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q49
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: Two identical pipes (i.e., having the same length, same diameter, and same roughness) are used to withdraw water from a reservoir. In the first case, they are attached in series and discharge freely into the atmosphere. In the second case, they are attached in parallel and also discharge freely into the atmosphere. Neglecting all minor losses, and assuming that the friction factor is same in both the cases, the ratio of the discharge in the parallel arrangement to that in the series arrangement (round off to 2 decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pipe Flow (Pipes in Series and Parallel)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Two identical pipes: Length \(L\), Diameter \(D\), Friction factor \(f\)
    • Case 1: Attached in Series. Discharge \(= Q_s\)
    • Case 2: Attached in Parallel. Discharge \(= Q_p\)
    • Both cases withdraw from the same reservoir under constant head \(H\). Minor losses neglected.
  • Aim: Ratio of discharge \(Q_p / Q_s\).

3. Core Concepts:

Darcy-Weisbach Equation: In terms of discharge \(Q\):

\[h_f = \dfrac{8 f L Q^2}{\pi^2 g D^5} = k L Q^2 \]

where \(k = \dfrac{8f}{\pi^2 g D^5}\) is a constant for identical pipes.

Series Arrangement: Total head loss is the sum of individual pipe losses. Discharge \(Q_s\) is uniform throughout.

Parallel Arrangement: Head loss across each pipe equals \(H\). Total discharge \(Q_p\) is the sum of individual branch discharges.

4. Solution Method & Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Series Case\[H = kLQ_s^2 + kLQ_s^2 = 2kLQ_s^2 \implies Q_s = \sqrt{\dfrac{H}{2kL}} \]
  2. Step 2: Parallel Case
    Head loss in each branch:\[H = kLQ_{p1}^2 \implies Q_{p1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{H}{kL}} \]Total discharge:\[Q_p = 2Q_{p1} = 2\sqrt{\dfrac{H}{kL}} \]
  3. Step 3: Calculate the Ratio\[\dfrac{Q_p}{Q_s} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{\dfrac{H}{kL}}}{\sqrt{\dfrac{H}{2kL}}} = \dfrac{2}{1/\sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2} = 2 \times 1.414 = 2.828 \approx 2.83 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2.83 | Accepted key range: 2.80 to 2.90

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The ordinates, u, of a 2-hour unit hydrograph (i.e., for 1 cm of effective rain), for a catchment are shown in the table.
t (hour)0123456789101112
u (m³/s)0281832453019127310

A 6-hour storm occurs over the catchment such that the effective rainfall intensity is 1 cm/hour for the first two hours, zero for the next two hours, and 0.5 cm/hour for the last two hours. If the base flow is constant at 5 m³/s, the peak flow due to this storm (in m³/s, round off to 1 decimal place) will be ______
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Hydrographs (Unit Hydrograph)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Ordinates of a 2-hour Unit Hydrograph (UH) for 1 cm effective rain
    • Base flow \(= 5\) m³/s (constant)
    • 6-hour storm (in 2-hour blocks):
      • 0–2 hr: Intensity \(i_1 = 1\) cm/h
      • 2–4 hr: Intensity \(i_2 = 0\) cm/h
      • 4–6 hr: Intensity \(i_3 = 0.5\) cm/h
  • Aim: Find the peak flow (Total Discharge) due to this storm.

3. Core Concepts:

Effective Rainfall (ER): \(ER = \text{Intensity} \times \text{Duration}\)

Superposition Principle: The Direct Runoff Hydrograph (DRH) is obtained by multiplying each ER depth with the shifted UH ordinates and summing them.

Total Flow: Peak Flow = Maximum DRH + Base Flow.

4. Solution Method & Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Calculate Effective Rainfall (ER) for each 2-hour block
    • \(ER_1\) (0–2 hr) \(= 1 \times 2 = 2\) cm
    • \(ER_2\) (2–4 hr) \(= 0 \times 2 = 0\) cm
    • \(ER_3\) (4–6 hr) \(= 0.5 \times 2 = 1\) cm
  2. Step 2: Superimpose the Unit Hydrograph ordinates\[DR(t) = ER_1 \cdot U(t) + ER_2 \cdot U(t-2) + ER_3 \cdot U(t-4) = 2\,U(t) + 0 + 1\,U(t-4) \]
  3. Step 3: Tabulate combined DRH ordinates around the peak
    Time (hr)\(2 \cdot U(t)\)\(1 \cdot U(t-4)\)DR(t) (m³/s)
    42(32) = 641(0) = 064
    52(45) = 901(2) = 292
    62(30) = 601(8) = 868
    72(19) = 381(18) = 1856
    82(12) = 241(32) = 3256
    92(7) = 141(45) = 4559
    Maximum direct runoff \(= 92\) m³/s at \(t = 5\) hours.
  4. Step 4: Calculate Peak Flow\[\text{Peak Flow} = 92 + 5 = 97\text{ m}^3\text{/s} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 97.0 m³/s | Accepted key range: 96.5 to 97.5

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q12
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: Bernoulli’s equation is applicable for
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Fluid Dynamics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Aim: Identify the fluid properties and flow conditions for which Bernoulli's equation is applicable.

3. Core Concepts:

Bernoulli's Equation is derived from conservation of energy applied to fluid flow. Its standard assumptions are:

  • Fluid is inviscid (frictionless, \(\mu = 0\))
  • Fluid is incompressible (\(\rho = \text{constant}\))
  • Flow is steady (\(\partial v / \partial t = 0\))
  • Applied along a streamline

4. Solution Method:

Evaluate each option against these standard assumptions.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  • Option (A): Viscous and compressible — Incorrect. Viscosity causes energy losses not accounted for in the standard form.
  • Option (B): Inviscid and compressible — Incorrect. Standard form assumes constant (incompressible) density.
  • Option (C): Inviscid and incompressible — Correct. Matches the standard ideal fluid flow assumptions.
  • Option (D): Viscous and incompressible — Incorrect. Viscous flow requires an energy loss term: \(\dfrac{P_1}{\gamma} + \dfrac{v_1^2}{2g} + z_1 = \dfrac{P_2}{\gamma} + \dfrac{v_2^2}{2g} + z_2 + h_L\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Inviscid and incompressible fluid flow | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q17
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A flow field is given by \( u = y^2 \), \( v = -xy \), \( w = 0 \). Value of the z-component of the angular velocity (in radians per unit time, up to two decimal places) at the point \( (0, -1, 1) \) is _______
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Kinematics of Flow: Angular Velocity

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Velocity field: \(u = y^2, v = -xy, w = 0\)
    Point of interest: \((0, -1, 1)\)
  • Aim: Determine z-component of angular velocity \(\omega_z\) (rad/unit time)

3. Core Concepts:

  • Angular velocity vector \(\vec{\omega} = \dfrac{1}{2}(\nabla \times \vec{V})\)
  • Z-component formula: \(\omega_z = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)\)
  • Standard assumption: Flow is continuous and differentiable

4. Solution Method:

  • Compute partial derivatives of velocity components
  • Substitute into angular velocity formula
  • Evaluate at given coordinates
  • Pitfall Alert: Sign convention in curl operation; remember the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) factor

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Compute partial derivatives:
    \[\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(-xy) = -y \]
    \[\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(y^2) = 2y \]
  2. Apply angular velocity formula:
    \[ \omega_z = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}[-y - 2y] = \dfrac{1}{2}(-3y) = -\dfrac{3y}{2} \]
  3. Evaluate at point \((0, -1, 1)\) where \(y = -1\):
    \[\omega_z = -\dfrac{3(-1)}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2} = 1.50 \text{ rad/unit time} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer(for NAT): \(1.50\) rad/unit time | Accepted range: 1.50 to 1.50

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q22
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A 1:50 model of a spillway is to be tested in the laboratory. The discharge in the prototype spillway is 1000 m³/s. The corresponding discharge (in m³/s, up to two decimal places) to be maintained in the model, neglecting variation in acceleration due to gravity, is _______
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Hydraulic Similitude: Froude Scaling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Scale ratio (model:prototype) \(L_r = 1:50\)
    Prototype discharge \(Q_p = 1000 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
    Gravity variation neglected (\(g_m = g_p\))
  • Aim: Determine model discharge \(Q_m\) (m³/s)

3. Core Concepts:

  • Froude number similarity for free-surface flows: \(Fr_m = Fr_p\)
  • Discharge scale ratio derivation:
    \[\dfrac{Q_m}{Q_p} = \left(\dfrac{L_m}{L_p}\right)^{5/2} = L_r^{5/2} \]
  • Key assumption: Spillway flow is gravity-dominated; viscous/surface tension effects negligible

4. Solution Method:

  • Apply Froude scaling law for discharge
  • Compute \(L_r^{5/2}\) carefully
  • Pitfall Alert: Exponent is 5/2 (not 2 or 3); ensure model:prototype ratio direction is correct

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Establish scale ratio:
    \[L_r = \dfrac{L_m}{L_p} = \dfrac{1}{50} \]
  2. Apply discharge scaling law:
    \[\dfrac{Q_m}{Q_p} = L_r^{5/2} = \left(\dfrac{1}{50}\right)^{5/2} = \dfrac{1}{50^{2.5}} \]
  3. Compute \(50^{2.5}\):
    \[50^{2.5} = 50^2 \times 50^{0.5} = 2500 \times \sqrt{50} = 2500 \times 7.07107 = 17677.67 \]
  4. Calculate model discharge:
    \[Q_m = Q_p \times \dfrac{1}{17677.67} = \dfrac{1000}{17677.67} = 0.05657 \text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]
  5. Round to two decimals:
    \[Q_m \approx 0.06 \text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer(for NAT): \(0.06\) m³/s | Accepted range: 0.05 to 0.06

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q23
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A 10 m wide rectangular channel carries a discharge of 20 m³/s under critical condition. Using \( g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2 \), the specific energy (in m, up to two decimal places) is _______
questions.explanation:
Open Channel Flow | Critical Flow & Specific Energy

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Rectangular channel width \(B = 10 \text{ m}\)
    Discharge \(Q = 20 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
    Critical flow condition
    \(g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2\)
  • Aim: Calculate specific energy \(E\) at critical flow (m)

3. Core Concepts:

  • Unit discharge: \(q = Q/B\)
  • Critical depth for rectangular channel: \(y_c = \left(\dfrac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3}\)
  • Specific energy at critical flow: \(E_c = y_c + \dfrac{V_c^2}{2g} = \dfrac{3}{2}y_c\) (key simplification)
  • Fundamental principle: At critical flow, Froude number \(Fr = 1\)

4. Solution Method:

  • Compute unit discharge \(q\)
  • Calculate critical depth \(y_c\)
  • Apply \(E_c = 1.5y_c\) relationship
  • Alternative: Compute \(V_c = q/y_c\) then \(E_c = y_c + V_c^2/(2g)\) for verification

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate unit discharge:
    \[q = \dfrac{Q}{B} = \dfrac{20}{10} = 2 \text{ m}^2/\text{s} \]
  2. Compute critical depth \(y_c\):
    \[y_c = \left(\dfrac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\dfrac{2^2}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\dfrac{4}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = (0.407747)^{1/3} \]
    \[y_c = 0.7415 \text{ m} \]
  3. Apply specific energy formula for critical flow:
    \[E_c = \dfrac{3}{2}y_c = 1.5 \times 0.7415 = 1.1123 \text{ m} \]
  4. Round to two decimals:
    \[E_c \approx 1.11 \text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer(for NAT): \(1.11\) m | Accepted range: 1.10 to 1.20

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q24
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: For routing of flood in a given channel using the Muskingum method, two of the routing coefficients are estimated as \( C_0 = -0.25 \) and \( C_1 = 0.55 \). The value of the third coefficient \( C_2 \) would be _______
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Flood Routing: Muskingum Method

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall/Application
  • Given Data:
    Muskingum coefficients: \(C_0 = -0.25, C_1 = 0.55\)
  • Aim: Determine third coefficient \(C_2\)

3. Core Concepts:

  • Muskingum routing equation: \(O_2 = C_0I_2 + C_1I_1 + C_2O_1\)
  • Fundamental constraint: Coefficients must sum to unity for mass conservation
    \[C_0 + C_1 + C_2 = 1 \]
  • Derived from continuity equation and storage-discharge relationship \(S = K[xI + (1-x)O]\)

4. Solution Method:

  • Apply coefficient summation constraint
  • Solve algebraically for \(C_2\)
  • Sanity Check: Coefficients should typically satisfy \(0 \leq C_1, C_2 \leq 1\); \(C_0\) can be negative for certain \(x\) values

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Apply mass conservation constraint:
    \[C_0 + C_1 + C_2 = 1 \]
  2. Substitute known values:
    \[-0.25 + 0.55 + C_2 = 1 \]
  3. Solve for \(C_2\):
    \[0.30 + C_2 = 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad C_2 = 1 - 0.30 = 0.70 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer(for NAT): \(0.70\) | Accepted range: 0.70 to 0.70

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q32
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A closed tank contains 0.5 m thick layer of mercury (specific gravity = 13.6) at the bottom. A 2.0 m thick layer of water lies above the mercury layer. A 3.0 m thick layer of oil (specific gravity = 0.6) lies above the water layer. The space above the oil layer contains air under pressure. The gauge pressure at the bottom of the tank is 196.2 kN/m². The density of water is 1000 kg/m³ and the acceleration due to gravity is 9.81 m/s². The value of pressure in the air space is
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Hydrostatics

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Mercury layer: \(h_{Hg} = 0.5 \text{ m}\), Specific Gravity \(S_{Hg} = 13.6\)
    • Water layer: \(h_w = 2.0 \text{ m}\), Specific Gravity \(S_w = 1.0\)
    • Oil layer: \(h_{oil} = 3.0 \text{ m}\), Specific Gravity \(S_{oil} = 0.6\)
    • Unit weight of water: \(\gamma_w = 9.81 \text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • Gauge pressure at bottom: \(P_{bottom} = 196.2 \text{ kN/m}^2\)
  • Aim: Find the gauge pressure of the air space (\(P_{air}\)).

2. Core Concepts:

Using the Hydrostatic Law, the pressure at the bottom of the tank is the sum of the air pressure and the pressures exerted by each fluid column:

\[P_{bottom} = P_{air} + P_{oil} + P_{water} + P_{Hg} \]\[P = \gamma \cdot h = (S \cdot \gamma_w) \cdot h \]

3. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Calculate hydrostatic pressures of liquids\[P_{oil} = (0.6 \times 9.81) \times 3.0 = 17.658 \text{ kN/m}^2 \]\[P_{water} = (1.0 \times 9.81) \times 2.0 = 19.62 \text{ kN/m}^2 \]\[P_{Hg} = (13.6 \times 9.81) \times 0.5 = 66.708 \text{ kN/m}^2 \]
  2. Step 2: Setup Equation and Solve\[P_{bottom} = P_{air} + P_{oil} + P_{water} + P_{Hg} \]\[196.2 = P_{air} + 17.658 + 19.62 + 66.708 \]\[196.2 = P_{air} + 103.986 \]\[P_{air} = 196.2 - 103.986 = 92.214 \text{ kN/m}^2 \]

4. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 92.214 kN/m² | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Rainfall depth over a watershed is monitored through six number of well distributed rain gauges. Gauged data are given below

Rain Gauge Number123456
Rainfall Depth (mm)470465435525480510
Area of Thiessen Polygon (×10⁴ m²)9510098808592


The Thiessen mean value (in mm, up to one decimal place) of the rainfall is _______
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Precipitation

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Six rain gauges with recorded rainfall depths \(P_i\) (mm) and Thiessen polygon areas \(A_i\) (\(\times 10^4 \text{ m}^2\)):
    Gauge\(P_i\) (mm)\(A_i\) (\(\times 10^4 \text{ m}^2\))
    147095
    2465100
    343598
    452580
    548085
    651092
  • Aim: Calculate the Thiessen mean rainfall over the watershed (mm, to one decimal place).

3. Core Concepts:

The Thiessen Polygon method assigns an area of influence to each rain gauge. The mean precipitation is the area-weighted average:

\[\bar{P} = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (P_i \times A_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i} \]

Note: Since all areas share the multiplier \(10^4 \text{ m}^2\), it cancels in numerator and denominator — raw integer values are used directly.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Sum all polygon areas to get \(A_{total}\).
  2. Compute \(P_i \times A_i\) for each gauge and sum them.
  3. Divide by \(A_{total}\) to get \(\bar{P}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Total Area\[A_{total} = 95 + 100 + 98 + 80 + 85 + 92 = 550 \]
  2. Step 2: Area-Weighted Rainfall Sum
    Gauge\(P_i \times A_i\)
    1\(470 \times 95 = 44{,}650\)
    2\(465 \times 100 = 46{,}500\)
    3\(435 \times 98 = 42{,}630\)
    4\(525 \times 80 = 42{,}000\)
    5\(480 \times 85 = 40{,}800\)
    6\(510 \times 92 = 46{,}920\)
    Total263,500
  3. Step 3: Mean Rainfall\[\bar{P} = \dfrac{263{,}500}{550} = 479.09 \approx 479.1 \text{ mm} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 479.1 mm | Accepted key range: 478.5 to 479.5

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q49
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The infiltration rate \( f \) in a basin under ponding condition is given by \( f = 30 + 10e^{-2t} \), where, \( f \) is in mm/h and \( t \) is time in hour. Total depth of infiltration (in mm, up to one decimal place) during the last 20 minutes of a storm of 30 minutes duration is _______
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Infiltration

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Horton's infiltration equation: \(f = 30 + 10e^{-2t}\) (\(f\) in mm/h, \(t\) in hours)
    • Storm duration: 30 minutes
  • Aim: Find the total depth of infiltration (mm) during the last 20 minutes of the storm.

3. Core Concepts:

To find total infiltration depth over a time window, integrate the rate equation:

\[F = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} f(t)\, dt \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert all times to hours (since \(t\) in the equation is in hours).
  2. The last 20 minutes of a 30-minute storm = interval from \(t_1 = 10 \text{ min} = 1/6 \text{ h}\) to \(t_2 = 30 \text{ min} = 1/2 \text{ h}\).
  3. Set up and evaluate the definite integral analytically.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Setup the Integral\[F = \int_{1/6}^{1/2} (30 + 10e^{-2t})\, dt \]
  2. Step 2: Integrate\[ F = \left[30t - 5e^{-2t} \right]_{1/6}^{1/2} \]
  3. Step 3: Evaluate Upper Limit (\(t = 1/2\))\[F_{upper} = 30\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) - 5e^{-1} = 15 - \dfrac{5}{2.7183} = 15 - 1.8394 = 13.1606 \text{ mm} \]
  4. Step 4: Evaluate Lower Limit (\(t = 1/6\))\[F_{lower} = 30\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right) - 5e^{-1/3} = 5 - 5(0.7165) = 5 - 3.5826 = 1.4174 \text{ mm} \]
  5. Step 5: Total Depth\[F = 13.1606 - 1.4174 = 11.7432 \approx 11.7 \text{ mm} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 11.7 mm | Accepted key range: 11.0 to 12.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: In a laboratory, a flow experiment is performed over a hydraulic structure. The measured values of discharge and velocity are 0.05 m³/s and 0.25 m/s, respectively. If the full scale structure (30 times bigger) is subjected to a discharge of 270 m³/s, then the time scale (model to full scale) value (up to two decimal places) is _______
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Dimensional Analysis & Model Studies

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Model Discharge: \(Q_m = 0.05 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
    • Model Velocity: \(v_m = 0.25 \text{ m/s}\)
    • Scale Ratio: \(L_r = L_m / L_p = 1/30\)
    • Prototype Discharge: \(Q_p = 270 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
  • Aim: Find the time scale ratio \(T_r = T_m / T_p\).

3. Core Concepts:

The dimensions of discharge are \([Q] = L^3 T^{-1}\), so:

\[Q_r = \dfrac{L_r^3}{T_r} \implies T_r = \dfrac{L_r^3}{Q_r} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Find the discharge ratio \(Q_r = Q_m / Q_p\).
  2. Use the kinematic relationship to isolate \(T_r\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Discharge Scale Ratio\[Q_r = \dfrac{Q_m}{Q_p} = \dfrac{0.05}{270} = \dfrac{1}{5400} \]
  2. Step 2: Time Scale Ratio\[T_r = \dfrac{L_r^3}{Q_r} = \dfrac{(1/30)^3}{1/5400} = \dfrac{1/27{,}000}{1/5400} = \dfrac{5400}{27{,}000} = \dfrac{1}{5} = 0.20 \]

Sanity Check via Velocity: If \(T_r = 0.2\), then \(V_r = L_r / T_r = (1/30)/(1/5) = 1/6\). Given \(v_m = 0.25 \text{ m/s}\), prototype velocity \(v_p = 0.25 \times 6 = 1.5 \text{ m/s}\). Then \(Q_p = 900 \times A_m \times 1.5 = 1350 \times (0.05/0.25) = 270 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}\). ✓

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.20 | Accepted key range: 0.15 to 0.25

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q12
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: Dupuit's assumptions are valid for
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Well Hydraulics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: Types of aquifers — Artesian, Confined, Leaky, Unconfined.
  • Aim: Identify the aquifer type for which Dupuit's assumptions are valid.

3. Core Concepts:

Dupuit's Assumptions (1863):

  • The flow is horizontal and uniform in any vertical section.
  • The velocity of flow is proportional to the tangent of the hydraulic gradient (slope of the free water surface).
  • The curvature of the free surface is small and can be neglected.

Solution Methods by Aquifer Type:

Aquifer TypeApplicable Theory
UnconfinedDupuit's Theory
Confined / ArtesianTheis / Theim Solution
LeakyHantush-Jacob Solution

4. Solution Method:

Dupuit's assumptions are fundamentally made for flow towards a well in an unconfined aquifer (water table aquifer), where the free surface (water table) slopes towards the well and gravity drainage is the mechanism of storage release. These assumptions allow approximating the complex 3D flow near the well as simplified 2D horizontal flow.

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Unconfined aquifer | Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q13
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: For a given discharge in an open channel, there are two depths which have the same specific energy. These two depths are known as
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow — Specific Energy

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: Two depths \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) have the same specific energy \(E\).
  • Aim: Identify the correct terminology for these depths.

3. Core Concepts:

Specific Energy (\(E\)):\[E = y + \dfrac{V^2}{2g} = y + \dfrac{Q^2}{2gA^2}\]

Key Depths on the Specific Energy Curve:

TermDefinition
Critical Depth (\(y_c\))Depth at which specific energy is minimum (\(E_{min}\))
Alternate DepthsTwo depths (one subcritical, one supercritical) having the same specific energy \(E > E_{min}\)
Sequent DepthsTwo depths conjugate to each other in a hydraulic jump (related to specific force, not specific energy)
Normal DepthDepth for uniform flow determined by Manning's / Chezy's equation

4. Solution Method:

On the specific energy curve, draw a horizontal line at energy \(E > E_{min}\). It intersects the curve at two points: one at \(y_{subcritical}\) (high depth, low velocity) and one at \(y_{supercritical}\) (low depth, high velocity). These two depths are defined as Alternate Depths.

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Alternate depths | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q24
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The intensity of irrigation for the Kharif season is 50% for an irrigation project with culturable command area of 50,000 hectares. The duty for the Kharif season is 1000 hectare/cumec. Assuming transmission loss of 10%, the required discharge (in cumec, up to two decimal places) at the head of the canal is ______
questions.explanation:
Irrigation Engineering | Canal Discharge Calculation with Transmission Losses

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Culturable Command Area (CCA) = 50,000 hectares
    • Intensity of irrigation (Kharif) = 50%
    • Duty at field (Kharif) = 1000 hectare/cumec
    • Transmission loss = 10% → Efficiency \(\eta = 90\%\)
  • Aim: Calculate required discharge at canal head (in cumec).

3. Core Concepts:

Area to be irrigated: \(A = \text{CCA} \times \text{Intensity}\)

Duty (\(D\)): Area irrigated per unit discharge (hectare/cumec).\[Q_{field} = \dfrac{A}{D}\]

Transmission efficiency:\[\eta = \dfrac{Q_{field}}{Q_{head}} \implies Q_{head} = \dfrac{Q_{field}}{\eta}\]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Area to be irrigated:\[A = 50{,}000 \times 0.50 = 25{,}000\text{ ha}\]
  2. Discharge at field level:\[Q_{field} = \dfrac{25{,}000}{1000} = 25\text{ cumec}\]
  3. Account for transmission loss:\[\eta = 1 - 0.10 = 0.90\]
  4. Discharge at canal head:\[Q_{head} = \dfrac{25}{0.90} = 27.78\text{ cumec}\]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 27.78 cumec | Accepted range: 27.00 to 28.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q25
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A culvert is designed for a flood frequency of 100 years and a useful life of 20 years. The risk involved in the design of the culvert (in percentage, up to two decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Hydrology & Water Resources | Risk Analysis in Hydraulic Structure Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Design flood return period: \(T = 100\text{ years}\)
    • Useful life of structure: \(n = 20\text{ years}\)
  • Aim: Calculate design risk percentage (to two decimal places).

3. Core Concepts:

Annual exceedance probability: \(p = \dfrac{1}{T}\)

Risk (\(R\)): Probability that the design event is exceeded at least once in \(n\) years (Bernoulli trials; flood events are assumed independent year-to-year).\[R = 1 - (1 - p)^n\]

Pitfall: Do not use \(R = n/T\) (linear approximation, invalid for \(n/T > 0.1\)).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Annual exceedance probability:\[p = \dfrac{1}{100} = 0.01\]
  2. Apply risk formula for \(n = 20\):\[R = 1 - (1 - 0.01)^{20} = 1 - (0.99)^{20}\]
  3. Compute \((0.99)^{20}\):\[(0.99)^{20} = 0.81791\](Using: \(\ln(0.99^{20}) = 20 \times \ln(0.99) = 20 \times (-0.01005) = -0.2010\); \(e^{-0.2010} = 0.8179\))
  4. Calculate risk:\[R = 1 - 0.81791 = 0.18209\]
  5. Convert to percentage:\[R\% = 0.18209 \times 100 = 18.21\%\]

Sanity Check: For \(T = 100\), \(n = 20\), risk ≈ 18–19% (not the 20% linear approximation). ✓

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 18.21% | Accepted range: 17.50 to 18.50

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: In a 5 m wide rectangular channel, the velocity u distribution in the vertical direction y is given by \( u = 1.25y^{\frac{1}{6}} \). The distance y is measured from the channel bed. If the flow depth is 2 m, the discharge per unit width of the channel is
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Channel width: \(B = 5\text{ m}\)
    • Velocity distribution: \(u(y) = 1.25\, y^{1/6}\text{ m/s}\) (where \(y\) is distance from the bed)
    • Flow depth: \(h = 2\text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the discharge per unit width (\(q\)) in \(\text{m}^3\text{/s/m}\).

3. Core Concepts:

Discharge per Unit Width (\(q\)): Represents the integration of the velocity profile over the entire depth of flow.\[q = \int_{0}^{h} u(y)\, dy\]

4. Solution Method:

Direct integration of the given power-law velocity distribution formula with respect to \(y\), evaluated from the bed (\(y = 0\)) to the free surface (\(y = 2\text{ m}\)).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Set up the integral:\[q = \int_{0}^{2} 1.25\, y^{1/6}\, dy\]
  2. Integrate:\[q = 1.25 \left[\dfrac{y^{\dfrac{1}{6}+1}}{\dfrac{1}{6}+1} \right]_{0}^{2} = 1.25 \left[\dfrac{y^{7/6}}{7/6} \right]_{0}^{2}\]\[q = 1.25 \times \dfrac{6}{7} \left[y^{7/6} \right]_{0}^{2} = \dfrac{7.5}{7} \left( 2^{7/6} - 0 \right)\]
  3. Calculate the final value:\[2^{7/6} = 2^1 \times 2^{1/6} \approx 2 \times 1.12246 = 2.2449\]\[q = \left(\dfrac{7.5}{7}\right) \times 2.2449 \approx 1.0714 \times 2.2449 = 2.405\text{ m}^3\text{/s/m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2.40 \(\text{m}^3\text{/s/m}\) | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q46
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A three-fluid system (immiscible) is connected to a vacuum pump. The specific gravity values of the fluids (S₁, S₂) are given in the figure.



The gauge pressure value (in kN/m², up to two decimal places) of p₁ is ______
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Manometry & Hydrostatics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Fluid I: \(S_1 = 0.88\)
    • Fluid II: \(S_2 = 0.95\)
    • Fluid III (Water): \(\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • \(p_{atm} = 95.43\text{ kPa}\)
    • Heights from diagram: Fluid III interface at \(0.5\text{ m}\), Fluid II interface at \(1.0\text{ m}\), Fluid I top surface at \(1.5\text{ m}\)
    • Outer reservoir free surface is at the same level as the \(0.5\text{ m}\) mark
  • Aim: Find the gauge pressure \(p_1\) inside the vacuum tank.

3. Core Concepts:

Hydrostatic Equation: For static fluids, pressure increases going down and decreases going up: \(\Delta p = \pm \gamma h\).

Pascal's Law in Manometry: Pressure in a continuous static fluid is equal at the same horizontal elevation.

Gauge vs Absolute: Gauge pressure equates atmospheric pressure to zero. The value \(95.43\text{ kPa}\) is a distractor meant for absolute pressure calculations.

4. Solution Method:

Since the outer reservoir surface is open to atmosphere and its level aligns with the \(0.5\text{ m}\) interface inside the central tank, the pressure at \(z = 0.5\text{ m}\) is precisely \(p_{atm}\) (or 0 gauge). Write the manometric equation from the vacuum pump (\(p_1\)) downwards to the \(0.5\text{ m}\) elevation.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify layer thicknesses inside the tank:
    • Thickness of Fluid I: \(h_1 = 1.5 - 1.0 = 0.5\text{ m}\)
    • Thickness of Fluid II: \(h_2 = 1.0 - 0.5 = 0.5\text{ m}\)
  2. Manometric Equation (start at \(p_1\) gauge and move down to \(z = 0.5\text{ m}\)):\[p_1 + (\gamma_1 \cdot h_1) + (\gamma_2 \cdot h_2) = p_{\text{at } 0.5\text{m}}\]Since \(p_{\text{at } 0.5\text{m, gauge}} = 0\):\[p_1 + (S_1 \cdot \gamma_w \cdot 0.5) + (S_2 \cdot \gamma_w \cdot 0.5) = 0\]
  3. Calculation:\[p_1 + (0.88 \times 9.81 \times 0.5) + (0.95 \times 9.81 \times 0.5) = 0\]\[p_1 + 4.3164 + 4.65975 = 0\]\[p_1 + 8.97615 = 0\]\[p_1 = -8.976\text{ kPa}\](A negative gauge pressure indicates a vacuum, which matches the diagram.)

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: −8.98 kN/m² | Accepted key range: −9.0 to −8.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q47
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The total rainfall in a catchment of area 1000 km², during a 6 h storm, is 19 cm. The surface runoff due to this storm computed from triangular direct runoff hydrograph is 1×10⁸ m³. The φindex for this storm (in cm/h, up to one decimal place) is ______
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Hydrographs & Infiltration

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Catchment area: \(A = 1000\text{ km}^2 = 10^9\text{ m}^2\)
    • Storm duration: \(t = 6\text{ h}\)
    • Total rainfall: \(P = 19\text{ cm}\)
    • Direct runoff volume: \(V = 1 \times 10^8\text{ m}^3\)
  • Aim: Calculate the \(\phi\)-index for the storm in cm/h.

3. Core Concepts:

Direct Runoff Depth (\(R\)):\[R = \dfrac{\text{Volume of Direct Runoff}}{\text{Catchment Area}}\]

\(\phi\)-index: Represents the average constant infiltration rate over the rainfall duration. Assuming uniform intensity and rainfall rate constantly exceeding infiltration:\[\phi_{\text{index}} = \dfrac{P - R}{t}\]

Note: Mention of "triangular DRH" specifies the hydrograph's shape, but since the raw volume is explicitly provided, shape parameters are irrelevant.

4. Solution Method:

Calculate the direct runoff depth in cm, determine the total infiltration depth, and divide by the time duration.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Runoff Depth (\(R\)):\[R = \dfrac{V}{A} = \dfrac{1 \times 10^8\text{ m}^3}{1 \times 10^9\text{ m}^2} = 0.1\text{ m} = 10\text{ cm}\]
  2. Calculate Total Infiltration:\[\text{Infiltration} = P - R = 19\text{ cm} - 10\text{ cm} = 9\text{ cm}\]
  3. Calculate \(\phi_{\text{index}}\):\[\phi_{\text{index}} = \dfrac{9\text{ cm}}{6\text{ h}} = 1.5\text{ cm/h}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.5 cm/h | Accepted key range: 1.50 to 1.50

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A rough pipe of 0.5 m diameter, 300 m length and roughness height of 0.25 mm, carries water (kinematic viscosity = 0.9×10⁻⁶ m²/s) with velocity of 3 m/s. Friction factor (f) for laminar flow is given by f = 64/Rₑ, and for turbulent flow it is given by \( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = 2\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{r}{k}\right)+1.74 \), where, Rₑ = Reynolds number, r = radius of pipe, k = roughness height and g = 9.81 m/s². The head loss (in m, up to three decimal places) in the pipe due to friction is ______
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Flow Through Pipes

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Diameter: \(D = 0.5\text{ m}\), Radius: \(r = 0.25\text{ m}\)
    • Length: \(L = 300\text{ m}\)
    • Roughness height: \(k = 0.25\text{ mm} = 0.25 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\)
    • Kinematic viscosity: \(\nu = 0.9 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}\), Velocity: \(v = 3\text{ m/s}\)
    • Formula provided: \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = 2\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{r}{k}\right) + 1.74\)
  • Aim: Compute the head loss (\(h_f\)) in metres due to friction.

3. Core Concepts:

Darcy-Weisbach Equation:\[h_f = \dfrac{f \cdot L \cdot v^2}{2 \cdot g \cdot D}\]where \(f\) is the Darcy friction factor.

Verification of flow regime:\[Re = \dfrac{v \cdot D}{\nu} = \dfrac{3 \times 0.5}{0.9 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.67 \times 10^6 > 4000\quad\text{(Fully turbulent)}\]

The empirical relation provided calculates the Darcy friction factor for rough turbulent pipes directly.

4. Solution Method:

Determine \(r/k\), substitute into the empirical friction factor equation to find \(f\). Then plug \(f\) into the Darcy-Weisbach equation to find \(h_f\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Relative Roughness Ratio (\(r/k\)):\[\dfrac{r}{k} = \dfrac{0.25}{0.25 \times 10^{-3}} = 1000\]
  2. Determine Friction Factor (\(f\)):\[\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = 2\log_{10}(1000) + 1.74 = 2(3) + 1.74 = 7.74\]\[\sqrt{f} = \dfrac{1}{7.74} = 0.129199\]\[f = (0.129199)^2 \approx 0.016692\]
  3. Compute Head Loss (\(h_f\)):\[h_f = \dfrac{f \cdot L \cdot v^2}{2 \cdot g \cdot D} = \dfrac{0.016692 \times 300 \times (3)^2}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.5}\]\[h_f = \dfrac{0.016692 \times 2700}{9.81} = \dfrac{45.0684}{9.81} = 4.594\text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 4.594 m | Accepted key range: 4.50 to 4.70

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q12
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: For a steady incompressible laminar flow between two infinite parallel stationary plates, the shear stress variation is
options: linear with zero value at the plates
linear with zero value at the center
quadratic with zero value at the plates
quadratic with zero value at the center

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: linear with zero value at the plates
structuredOptions.html: linear with zero value at the plates

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: linear with zero value at the center
structuredOptions.html: linear with zero value at the center

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: quadratic with zero value at the plates
structuredOptions.html: quadratic with zero value at the plates

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: quadratic with zero value at the center
structuredOptions.html: quadratic with zero value at the center

questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Viscous Flow (Laminar Flow)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Steady, incompressible, laminar flow between two infinite parallel stationary plates.
  • Aim: Determine the spatial variation (profile) of shear stress across the flow.

3. Core Concepts:

The Navier-Stokes equations simplify to:

\[\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} = \mu\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} \]

Integrating with respect to \(y\):

\[\tau = \mu\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}\right)y + C \]

Applying symmetry at the center (\(y = 0\), where \(du/dy = 0\)), \(C = 0\). Thus:

\[\tau = \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}\right)y \]

Since the pressure gradient is constant, shear stress varies linearly with \(y\).

4. Solution Method:

  • At center (\(y = 0\)): \(\tau = 0\)
  • At the plates: \(\tau\) is at maximum absolute value
  • Relationship \(\tau \propto y\) is linear

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Linear with zero value at the center  |  Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q23
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A triangular pipe network is shown in the figure.

The head loss in each pipe is given by \(h_f = r Q^{1.8}\), with the variables expressed in a consistent set of units. The value of \(r\) for the pipe \(AB\) is 1 and for the pipe \(BC\) is 2. If the discharge supplied at the point A (i.e., 100) is equally divided between the pipes AB and AC, the value of \(r\) (up to two decimal places) for the pipe AC should be _______________
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pipe Networks (Hardy Cross Principles)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Head loss equation: \(h_f = rQ^{1.8}\)
    • \(r_{AB} = 1\), \(r_{BC} = 2\)
    • Inflow at A: 100 units; Outflow at B: 70 units; Outflow at C: 30 units
    • Flow at A is equally divided between pipes AB and AC
  • Aim: Find the pipe resistance \(r_{AC}\) for pipe AC.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Continuity at Nodes (Kirchhoff's 1st Law): \(\sum Q_{in} = \sum Q_{out}\) at every junction.
  • Energy Conservation in Loops (Kirchhoff's 2nd Law): The head difference between any two nodes is path-independent:
    \[H_A - H_B = \sum h_f \text{ (along any path A to B)} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Use equal division condition at A to find \(Q_{AB}\) and \(Q_{AC}\).
  2. Apply continuity at Node B to find \(Q_{BC}\).
  3. Apply energy conservation between A and B via both paths.
  4. Solve for \(r_{AC}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Flows at Node A (equally divided):
    \[Q_{AB} = Q_{AC} = \dfrac{100}{2} = 50\text{ units} \]
  2. Flow in BC (continuity at Node B):
    Inflow to B from AB = 50; required outflow = 70 \(\implies\) additional inflow needed = 20.
    \[Q_{CB} = 20\text{ units (C to B)} \]
    Self-check at C: inflow = 50, outflow = 30 (external) + 20 (to B) = 50 ✓
  3. Energy balance (A to B via two paths):
    \[h_{f,AB} = h_{f,AC} + h_{f,CB} \]\[r_{AB}(Q_{AB})^{1.8} = r_{AC}(Q_{AC})^{1.8} + r_{BC}(Q_{CB})^{1.8} \]\[1 \times (50)^{1.8} = r_{AC} \times (50)^{1.8} + 2 \times (20)^{1.8} \]\[1148.698 = 1148.698\,r_{AC} + 2 \times 218.673 \]\[1148.698 = 1148.698\,r_{AC} + 437.346 \]\[r_{AC} = \dfrac{1148.698 - 437.346}{1148.698} = \dfrac{711.352}{1148.698} \approx 0.62 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.62  |  Accepted key range: 0.60 to 0.63
